paragraphs.text: Augustine, bishop, to his dearly beloved brothers who belong to the care of our stewardship: may the salvation that is in Christ, and the peace of his unity and love, be with you, and may your spirit, soul and body be kept whole for the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

You remember, brothers, that a very small part of a letter by Petilian, the Donatist bishop of Constantine, once came into our hands, and that I wrote to you, my beloved, what I had replied to that fragment. But when the whole letter, complete, was later sent to us by the brothers who are there, I decided to answer it from the beginning, as though we were dealing with each other face to face. You know that this is how we have always wanted to deal with them: without any zeal for contention, setting the arguments side by side, so that it may be plain to everyone what is said by them and what by us. We learned that the letter is in many people's hands, and that some even know much of it by heart, thinking that he said something true against us. But now, if they are willing to read what we have answered, they will surely understand what they ought to reject and what they ought to hold. For those answers are not ours, as they themselves can see if they are willing to judge without partisanship. Everything in them has been brought forward from the holy Scriptures and proved by them, so that no one can deny it except a man who declares himself an enemy of those Scriptures. But I see what the most stubborn defenders of so bad a cause can say about that work of ours: that I answered the letter of an absent man, who could not hear my words and reply to them at once. Let him, then, defend the words of his letter and, if he can, show that my replies did not refute and confute them. Or, if he does not want to do that, let him do to this letter of mine what I did to the letter of his that I have already answered. After all, he wrote that letter to his own people, as I write this one to you. Let him answer this one too, if he wishes.

The question between us is certainly where the Church is: with us or with them. It is, of course, the one Church that our forefathers named catholic, to show by the very name that it extends throughout the whole; for "according to the whole" is said in Greek kath' holon. This Church is the body of Christ, as the apostle says: "for the sake of his body, which is the Church." From this it is surely clear that whoever is not among the members of Christ cannot have Christian salvation. The members of Christ are joined to one another by the charity of unity, and by that same charity they cling to their head, which is Christ Jesus. Everything, then, that is proclaimed about Christ is head and body. The head is the only-begotten Jesus Christ himself, the Son of the living God, himself the savior of the body, who died for our sins and rose again for our justification. His body is the Church, of which it is said: "that he might present to himself a glorious Church, without spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind." Between us and the Donatists, then, the question is where this body is, that is, where the Church is. What, then, shall we do? Shall we look for it in our own words, or in the words of its head, our Lord Jesus Christ? I think we ought rather to look for it in his words, for he is the truth and knows his own body best: "the Lord knows those who are his."

Notice which words are ours, in which the Church must not be sought, and see even there how our words differ from theirs. Still, we do not want the Church to be sought in our words. Whatever we charge against each other about handing over the divine books, about burning incense, or about persecutions, these are our words. In such matters we hold to this method. Both sets of charges may be reckoned true, ours and theirs alike; or both false; or ours true and theirs false; or ours false and theirs true. In every one of these cases we show that the Christian world with which we are in communion is guilty of no crime. If the crimes we allege against them and the crimes they allege against us are both true, let us do as the apostle says: "forgiving one another, as God in Christ has forgiven us." Then wicked men, neither those who perhaps were or are among us nor those who were or are among them, will not hinder our concord and the bond of peace, once their one wickedness is corrected: that they separated themselves to no purpose from the unity of the whole world, while they had such men among themselves. But if both are false, whether what we charge them with or what they charge us with, about handing over the books or about persecuting the innocent, I see no cause for dispute, except that there is cause for those who separated themselves without cause to correct themselves. Suppose, however, that we speak the truth. We confirm it by the records we produce, by the letters of the emperor to whom they both first wrote at that time and later appealed, and by the communion of the whole world. What they say is proved false precisely because, at that very time, when the same question was being argued, they could not win their case at all. In that case they show a greater fury of sacrilegious hostility, and a greater persecution of innocent souls, than if they were guilty only of the crime of schism. Those crimes they may attribute not to all their people, but to whichever of them they please; schism, however, is the crime of all of them. Further, suppose they want the charges of handing over and persecution that they bring to be true, and the charges we bring to be false. Even so they are not cleared of the crime of schism, for those charges can apply to certain individuals, not to the whole Christian world. If they think that the world has perished through contagion, I pass over how many evils the saints tolerated in the human community for the sake of peace, even when those evils were known. I say only this: let them show how they themselves have not perished through the contagion of those sacrilegious men who defiled the consecrated chastity of women, men whom they either do not know, or once did not know, to be or to have been hiding among them. They will surely say that they were not contaminated precisely because they did not know. How, then, has the world been contaminated, when it still does not know whether what they say is true? Let us suppose it has now been proved to us, now demonstrated: what are we to do about so many nations? They would be deserted while they were ignorant; therefore they would be deserted while they were innocent. That would be no crime of theirs, but it would become a most wicked crime of ours. Or ought we to run and teach them what we know? To what end? If it is so that they may be innocent, they are innocent even while they do not know. We keep our innocence not by knowing the evil deeds of men, but by not consenting to them once they are known, and by not judging rashly about what is unknown. And so, as I said, the whole world is innocent, since it does not know the crimes these men allege against certain persons, even if they allege them truly. Those who separated themselves from these innocent people lost their own innocence by that very crime of separation and schism. And now they try to teach us that what they say against certain persons is true, in order to separate us from people against whom they have nothing true to say.

For this is what the whole world says to them, very brief in words but very strong in truth. The African bishops, as we know, were in conflict with one another. Suppose they could not settle the dissension that had arisen among them, whether by reconciling the parties in concord or by degrading those who contended wrongly, so that those who had the good cause might remain in communion with the whole world through the bond of unity. Then surely it remained for the bishops overseas, where the greatest part of the catholic Church was spread, to judge the dissensions of their African colleagues, at the instance, of course, of those who were accusing others of the crime of wrongful ordination. If this was not done, the fault lies with those by whom it ought to have been done, not with the whole world, which did not know what had not been brought before it. But if it was done, what sin did the Church's judges commit? Even if the crimes reported to them were true, they were not proved to them, and so the judges ought in no way to have condemned them. Could wicked men pollute judges to whom they could not be exposed? But suppose they were exposed to them, and the judges, through some sluggishness or connivance, would not remove such men from communion and by a perverse judgment even pronounced sentence in their favor. What sin did the whole world commit then? It did not know that the case had bad judges, and it believed that men had judged well when it could not judge them itself. Just as the wickedness of the accused, if it was hidden from the judges, certainly did not contaminate them, so too the wickedness of the judges, if there was any, could certainly not contaminate the whole world, since it was hidden from the world. With these innocent people, then, we innocently hold communion still today, not knowing what was done back then. Therefore, even if we had learned today that what they say against certain persons is true, there would be no reason for us to withdraw from the innocent, who do not know these things, and go over to people who are all entangled in the crime of schism. They are entangled in it precisely because they did what they urge us to do: not to tolerate the wicked, after the example of the apostles, but to desert the good, after the example of heretics. But let us suppose something that cannot happen: that the whole world could today come to know clearly, together with us, that the crimes of certain persons whom these men accuse are real. Could the world become any more innocent through this than it was before it knew? Just as the wicked could not stain it while they were unknown, even if they were still in this life, so those who have already departed this life cannot stain it even when they are known. Our cause, then, as it stands in our own words about the crimes of certain persons, which we charge against each other, is such that it remains unconquered even if we learn today that what we say against some of their people is false and what they say against some of ours is true. What answer, then, do they have, whether what we say is true and what they say is false, or both are false, or both are true? For they are defeated even on the very point that is the one thing they pray with all their hearts to have believed.

But, as I had begun to say, let us not listen to "You say this, I say that," but let us listen to "Thus says the Lord." There are certainly the Lord's books, whose authority we both accept, to which we both yield, and which we both serve. There let us seek the Church; there let us discuss our case. Here they will perhaps say, "Why do you look in the books that you handed over to the flames?" To this I answer, "Why are you afraid of these books being read, if you saved them from the flames?" Surely the man to be believed to have handed them over is the one who, when they are read, is shown not to agree with them. Or perhaps these books point out their betrayer as the Lord pointed out Judas. In that case, let them read in them, by name and explicitly, that either Caecilian or those who ordained him would betray those same books. If I do not anathematize them, let me be judged to have handed the books over along with them. But neither do we find in those books that those who ordained Majorinus are named as betrayers, although we cite this from other sources. Let us therefore set aside the things that we cite against each other not from the divine canonical books but from elsewhere. If they do not want them set aside, let them consider this. If both sets of charges are true, there was no cause for their separation, for they fled from men like those they had among themselves. If both are false, there was no cause for their separation, for they fled from men in whom they found no crime. If ours are true and theirs false, there was no cause for their separation, since they ought rather to have corrected themselves and remained in unity. And if ours are false and theirs true, there was no cause for their separation, since they ought not to have deserted the innocent world, to which they either would not or could not demonstrate these things.

Perhaps someone may ask me, "Why, then, do you want these things set aside, when your communion remains unconquered even if they are brought forward?" Because I do not want the holy Church to be shown by human documents, but by divine oracles. Suppose the holy Scriptures had marked out the Church in Africa alone, and among a few Cutzupitani or Montenses at Rome, and in the house or estate of one Spanish woman. Then, whatever else might be brought forward from other papers, no one would hold the Church but the Donatists. If holy Scripture confines it to a few Moors of the province of Caesarea, we must go over to [?]. If to a few people of Tripolitania, Byzacena and the Province, then the Maximianists have attained it. If to the East alone, it must be sought among the Arians, the Eunomians, the Macedonians and whatever others there are there. But who could list every single heresy of every single nation? If, however, the Church of Christ is marked out in all nations by the divine and most certain testimonies of the canonical Scriptures, then whatever is brought forward, and from wherever it is cited, by those who say, "Look, here is the Christ; look, there he is," let us rather listen, if we are his sheep, to the voice of our shepherd saying, "Do not believe it." For each of those sects is missing from many nations where this Church is, but this Church, which is everywhere, is found even where they are. So let us seek it in the holy canonical Scriptures.

The whole Christ is head and body: the head is the only-begotten Son of God, and the body is his Church, bridegroom and bride, two in one flesh. Whoever disagrees with the holy Scriptures about the head itself is not in the Church, even if found in every place where the Church is marked out. And again, whoever agrees with the holy Scriptures about the head itself but does not share in the unity of the Church is not in the Church, because such people disagree about the body of Christ, which is the Church, with the testimony of Christ himself. For example, some do not believe that Christ came in the flesh from the Virgin Mary, of the seed of David, as the Scripture of God most plainly says, or that he rose again in the very body in which he was crucified and buried. Even if they are found throughout all the lands where the Church is, they are certainly not in the Church, because they do not hold to the head of the Church itself, which is Christ Jesus. Nor are they misled by some obscurity in the divine Scriptures; they contradict their best-known and plainest testimonies. Others believe that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, as has been said, and rose again in the same flesh in which he was born and suffered. They believe that he is the Son of God, God with God, one with the Father, and the unchangeable Word of the Father, through whom all things were made. Yet they disagree about his body, which is the Church, so that their communion is not with the whole Church wherever it is spread, but is found in some separated part. It is plain that they are not in the catholic Church. Our question with the Donatists, then, is not about the head but about the body; that is, not about the Savior Jesus Christ himself, but about his Church. So let the head himself, about whom we agree, show us his body, about which we disagree, so that through his words we may at last stop disagreeing. He is the only-begotten Son and the Word of God. That is why even the holy prophets could not have spoken the truth unless the Truth itself, which is the Word of God, had revealed to them what to say and commanded them to say it. Accordingly, in earlier times the Word of God spoke through the prophets, then through himself, when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and then through the apostles, whom he sent to preach him, so that there might be salvation to the ends of the earth. In all of these, then, the Church must be sought.

Slanderers often take many things that were said against other people or for another purpose and turn them against whomever they please and toward whatever end they please. Many other things were set down figuratively and obscurely to exercise rational minds, in the form of a riddle or with the double meaning of an ambiguous sense, and people sometimes think that these agree with and fit a misleading interpretation. So I also declare and propose this: let us choose whatever passages are open and clear. If such passages were not found in the holy Scriptures, there would be no way at all to open what is closed and to shed light on what is obscure. For example, see how easy it is for us to say against them, or for them to say against us, what the Lord said to the Pharisees: "You are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people, but inside are full of dead men's bones and all uncleanness. So you also outwardly appear righteous to people, but inside you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity." Whether we say this against them or they say it against us, anyone of even moderately sound mind knows that, unless it is first proved by the clearest evidence who the people are who are unrighteous and pretend to be righteous, the words are spoken with abusive levity [?] rather than convincing truth. The Lord said those words against the Pharisees in a quite different way, as Lord: as one who knows the heart and all the secrets of men, and as witness and judge. We, however, must first find and show what we are accusing, or else we ourselves will rather be accused of the very grave crime of mad rashness. Of course, if they first show us to be such people, we must by no means refuse to be rebuked and crushed with such words of the holy Scriptures. Likewise, if we show them to be such people, it will equally be within our power to strike them, once they are exposed and convicted, with whatever rebukes of the Lord we choose.

In the same way, for the present we must set aside passages that are stated obscurely and wrapped in the veils of figures, which can be interpreted both in our favor and in theirs. It is indeed the task of sharp-witted people to weigh and decide which side interprets such passages more convincingly. But in a case that concerns whole peoples, we do not wish to stake our debate on contests of cleverness. None of us doubts that the Church was also prefigured by Noah's ark, while the historical truth of the events remains intact: the sinners were destroyed and the household of the righteous man was saved from the flood. Even this might perhaps seem a conjecture of human ingenuity, if the apostle Peter did not say so in his letter. But suppose one of us were to say something Peter did not say there: that every kind of animal was in the ark because it foretold that the Church would exist in all nations. The Donatists might perhaps see it differently and wish to interpret this in another way. Likewise, if they interpret something stated obscurely or ambiguously in support of their own view, and we are free to draw from it some other meaning that speaks in our favor, where will it end? For one of their bishops, when he was preaching to the people here at Hippo, as we have heard, said that Noah's ark was pitched on the inside so that it would not let out its own water, and on the outside so that it would not let in water from elsewhere. Clearly he wanted this interpretation to support two claims: that baptism cannot be believed to go out beyond the Church, and that baptism given outside it should not be accepted. He seemed to be saying something, and those who listened gladly applauded him. They did not think carefully about what they had heard, or they would have noticed something easy to notice: a joined wooden structure cannot let water in from the outside if it does not let it out from the inside, and if it lets water out on the inside, it follows that it also lets water in on the outside. But even if what he said were true of a structure of joined timbers, who would stop me, if I could, from saying something else about the ark pitched on both sides, so that it would be uncertain which of these meanings that thing signified, or perhaps some third meaning? For it is not absurd, and is even much more plausible, to say that the pitch signifies charity, since it is a powerful glue and burns with intense heat. Why else is it said in the psalm, "My soul is glued fast behind you," if not because of the most burning charity? Since we are commanded to have this charity toward one another and toward all, the ark was pitched both inside and outside. Or else, since it is written, "Charity bears all things," the very power of forbearance, which holds fast to unity, is signified by the pitch. The ark was smeared with it inside and outside because the wicked must be borne with both inside and outside, so that the joints of peace may not come apart. In this debate of ours, then, let us refrain from such interpretations and look for something clear by which the Church may be shown.

It is written in the book of Judges: "And Gideon said to the Lord: Since you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said, see, I am laying a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If dew forms on the fleece but the whole ground stays dry, I shall know that you are saving Israel by my hand, as you have said. And so it happened. Gideon rose early the next day and wrung out the fleece, and the dew ran out of the fleece, a basin full of water. Then Gideon said to the Lord: Do not let your anger blaze against me, Lord. Let me speak just once more, and make one more test with the fleece: let the fleece alone be dry, and let there be dew on all the ground. And that night God did so: the fleece alone was dry, and there was dew on all the ground." I do not see what else is figured and foretold here, unless we are to understand the threshing floor as the whole world and the place of the fleece as the people of Israel. For we know that this nation was once soaked, as if with heavenly dew, by the grace of the divine sacrament, while all the nations around it lacked this gift and so were, as it were, in drought. Among that people, however, this gift was in a fleece, that is, under a covering and in a kind of cloud of secrecy, because it had not yet been revealed. But now we see the whole world enriched with the dew now revealed through the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, which was then figured under that covering; and we see that nation, having lost the priesthood it once had because it does not understand Christ in the Scriptures, left behind as if in a dry fleece. Yet even though I do not see what else could be understood here, I do not want us to look for the Church in figures of this kind. Let us set aside for the moment everything that needs any interpretation, even of this sort. This is not because what is unravelled by interpreting such things, as if they were wrappings, is false, but because they require an interpreter at all. I do not want our wits to be pitted against each other over them. Rather, let the open truth cry out and shine; let it burst into stopped-up ears and strike the eyes of those who pretend not to see. Let no one look in its hiding places for room for his own false opinion. Let it confound every attempt at contradiction and crush every brazen face of shamelessness.

O Donatists, read Genesis: "By myself I have sworn, says the Lord, because you have done this thing and did not spare your most beloved son for my sake, I will surely bless you, and I will surely multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand on the seashore; and your offspring shall possess as an inheritance the cities of their enemies, and in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you obeyed my voice." What do you say to this? Or will you take up the Jews' perversity in arguing with us, and say that the offspring of Abraham is to be understood only as the people born of Abraham's flesh? But the Jews do not read the apostle Paul in their synagogues, whereas you read him in your conventicles. So let us hear what the apostle says, for we are now asking how the offspring of Abraham is to be understood: "Brothers," he says, "I speak in human terms. Even a man's will, once ratified, no one annuls or adds to. The promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say 'and to offsprings', as of many, but as of one, 'and to your offspring', who is Christ." See the offspring in whom all nations are blessed; see the covenant of God. Open your ears: "Even a man's will, once ratified," he says, "no one annuls or adds to." Why then do you annul God's covenant by saying that it has not been fulfilled in all nations, and that it has already perished from the nations in which the offspring of Abraham was? Why do you add to it by saying that Christ remains heir in no lands except where he could have Donatus as co-heir? We begrudge no one anything. Read us this from the Law, from the Prophets, from the Psalms, from the Gospel itself, from the apostolic letters. Read it, and we will believe, just as we read to you, both from Genesis and from the apostle, that in the offspring of Abraham, who is Christ, all nations are blessed.

Hear this same covenant made with Isaac, Abraham's son: "Now there was a famine in the land, besides the earlier famine that had occurred in the time of Abraham. And Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerar. And the Lord appeared to him and said: Do not go down into Egypt, but live in the land of which I shall tell you. Live in this land, and I will be with you and bless you. For to you and to your offspring I will give all this land, and I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father. I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven, and I will give to you and to your offspring all this land, and in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because Abraham your father obeyed my voice and kept my commandments, my righteous decrees and my statutes." Answer this. The offspring of Abraham is the very same offspring as that of Isaac, namely Christ. For what Christian of any kind does not know how Christ came in the flesh from the tribe of Judah through the virgin?

Hear this same covenant made with Jacob: "And Jacob went out from the well of the oath and set out for Haran. He came to a place and slept there, for the sun had set. He took one of the stones of the place, put it under his head and slept in that place. And he saw a vision: there was a ladder set up on the earth, its top reaching to heaven, and the angels of God were going up and coming down on it. And the Lord was leaning over it and said: I am the Lord, the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac; do not be afraid. The land on which you are sleeping I will give to you and to your offspring. Your offspring shall be like the sand of the earth, and it shall spread out over the sea and to the south and to the north and to the east; and in you and in your offspring all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed. And see, I am with you, guarding you on every way you go, and I will bring you back to this land, for I will not abandon you until I have done everything I have spoken to you." See what promise you are resisting! See how firm a covenant you are annulling! The Lord says, "I will not abandon you until I have done everything I have spoken to you," and you contradict him, telling us to believe you instead in whatever crime you charge against a world that is unknown to you and knows nothing of it, and not to believe God when he says, "I will not abandon you until I have done it."

Read to us from the canonical Scriptures that the men you accuse by name handed over the divine books. Read us something as plain as these passages we have read to you from Genesis. We are not asking you what is signified by the stone that Jacob put under his head when he slept, by the ladder set up on the earth with its top reaching to heaven, or by the angels of God going up and coming down on it. Let wiser and more learned men investigate these things and speak of them to a congregation at peace, where no shameless contradiction will clamour, arming its impudence with the obscurity of the mystery and the riddle of the passage. There is no lack of faithful hearts for the Lord to remind of what he said in the Gospel when he saw an Israelite in whom there was no guile (for Jacob, who saw this ladder, was himself called Israel). There is no lack, then, of people for the Lord himself to remind of it. For there he said, "You will see heaven opened and the angels of God going up and coming down upon the Son of Man", that is, upon the offspring of Abraham in whom all nations are blessed. But I do not press these things on those who refuse them. Here is what you must hear: "Your offspring shall be like the sand of the earth, and it shall spread out over the sea and to the south and to the north and to the east; and in you and in your offspring all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed." Show me this Church, if you have it. Show that you are in communion with all the nations which we now see being blessed in this offspring. Show us this Church, or else lay aside your fury and receive it, not from me, but from him in whom all nations are blessed. Let it suffice to have cited these passages from the first book of the Law; more will become clear to those who read without impious contention and with devout love.

What about the Prophets? How many and how clear are their testimonies to the Church spread among all nations throughout the whole world! I shall cite a few of them, leaving more for the careful leisure of those who read in the fear of God. Let us receive divine answers through the mouth of holy Isaiah and consult his lips as oracles of God. Let the spirited and ruinous battles of human quarrels fall silent. Let us bend our ear to the word of God. Let Isaiah say where, by God's revelation, he foresaw the holy Church, so that in the words of one who spoke of the future we may now see what is present: "The whole earth," he says, "is filled, so that they know the Lord, as abundant water covers the sea. And on that day there shall be the root of Jesse, he who shall rise to rule over the nations; in him the nations shall hope." No Christian of any kind is unaware that the root of Jesse is Christ, born of the line of David according to the flesh; and if anyone wants to quarrel, let him quarrel with the apostle, who uses this testimony in his letters. He also says: "Israel shall bud and blossom, and the world shall be filled with its fruit." Israel, of course, was the son of Isaac and the grandson of Abraham, to whom it was promised that in his offspring all nations would be blessed, an offspring the apostle interprets as Christ. And Christ came from the line of Abraham through Isaac and through Israel and onward, as the evangelist sets out the generations leading to Christ's birth. So whoever wants to argue against this, let him contradict the Gospel and deny that Christ came from the line of Israel, so that he can deny what Isaiah says: "Israel shall bud and blossom, and the world shall be filled with its fruit." He also says: "I, God, am the first, and in the things that are to come, I am. The nations saw and the ends of the earth were afraid." This is what Scripture says elsewhere: "the first and the last", so that he is Alpha and Omega, the letters in the sign of Christ known to all. For in place of "the last" there, here we have "and in the things that are to come, I am." So those who refuse to believe contradict this manifestation; indeed, they refuse to see the fulfilment, already under way, of what follows: "The nations saw and the ends of the earth were afraid." Again, a little later: "Jacob my servant, I will uphold him; Israel my chosen, my soul has accepted him. I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations. He will not cry out nor cease, nor will his voice be heard outside. A bruised reed he will not break, and smoking flax he will not quench, but he will bring forth judgment in truth. He will shine forth and will not be broken until he establishes judgment on the earth, and in his name the nations will hope." This testimony is to be understood of Christ, and it is quoted in the Gospel. Let whoever dares contradict it; but let whoever does not dare hope in him together with the nations, and not withdraw from the unity of the nations that hope in him; or, if he has withdrawn, let him return, so that he does not perish.

Isaiah also says: "And now thus says the Lord, who formed me in the womb to be his servant, to gather Jacob and Israel to him: I will draw near to him, and I shall be honoured before the Lord, and my God will be my strength. And he said to me: It shall be a very great thing for you to be called my servant, to establish the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the offspring of Israel. I have made you a covenant for the race, a light for the nations, so that you may be salvation to the ends of the earth." And a little later: "Thus says the Lord of Israel: At a most fitting time I have heard you, and on the day of salvation I have helped you." When the apostle Paul quoted these words, he certainly showed that they are fulfilled only in Christians, for he went on to say: "See, now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation." So let us hear what Isaiah adds: "I have given you," he says, "as a covenant for the nations, to settle the land and possess the inheritance of the desert." Then, after some intervening words, he goes on to say: "See, these will come from afar, these from the north and the sea, and others from the land of the Persians. Rejoice, O heavens, and be glad, O earth; let the mountains break forth into gladness, for God has had mercy on his people and has spoken to the lowly of his people. But Zion said: The Lord has abandoned me, and God has forgotten me. Can a woman forget her own son, or can she fail to have pity on the child of her womb? Now even if she should forget, I will never forget you, says the Lord. See, I have inscribed your walls on my hands; you are before my eyes for ever, and soon you will be built up by those by whom you were overthrown." Since, then, the apostle's words do not allow us to understand this of the Jewish people, but of the Christian people, what are we to understand by Isaiah's words in this passage, "and soon you will be built up by those by whom you were overthrown," if not that it was foretold so long beforehand that the kings of the earth, who at first persecuted the Church, would afterwards help it? But because many of them were going to die in their iniquities, he adds: "and those who laid you waste will depart from you." Then, because all nations would be joined to the Church, he goes on to say: "Lift up your eyes all around and see them all. As I live, says the Lord, you shall clothe yourself with all of them and arrange them like the ornaments of a new bride. For the places in you that were deserted and ruined and fallen will now be crowded to bursting by those who dwell there, and those who devoured you shall be put far from you. For the children you had lost will say in your ears: This place is too cramped for us; make room for us now where we may live. And you will say in your heart: Who has borne these for me, when I know that I was childless and a widow? Who then has brought these up for me? For I was left alone; where were these? Thus says the Lord: See, I will lift up my hands to the nations and my signal to the islands, and they will bring your sons in their arms and carry your daughters on their shoulders. Kings will be your foster fathers, and their princesses your nurses. Bowing their faces to the ground they will entreat you and lick the dust of your feet, and you will know that I am the Lord, and you will not be put to shame." And a little later he adds: "Hear me, hear me, my people; and you kings, give heed to me, for the law will go out from me and my judgment as a light to the nations. My righteousness draws near swiftly, and my salvation will go forth, and by my arm the nations are saved." Let us consult the apostolic Scriptures about this arm. For when the apostle Paul cited the testimony of this same prophet concerning the unbelief of the Jews, that Christ had not been revealed to them, he quoted this: "Who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" Then, in what follows, Isaiah adds: "Let the waste places of Jerusalem break out together in joy, for he has had mercy on her and has rescued Jerusalem; and the Lord will lay bare his holy arm in the sight of all the nations, and all nations to the ends of the earth will see the salvation that comes from God." Who is so deaf, who so mad, who so blind in mind as to speak against such evident testimonies, unless he does not know what he is saying?

But let us come to things still clearer. We certainly know from the Scriptures of that most holy marriage, the bridegroom and the bride, Christ and the Church. Isaiah writes of both, so that we may not go wrong about either of them; for whoever goes wrong about one loses both, since it is of this marriage that the mystery speaks, as the apostle testifies: "The two shall be one flesh." So the bridegroom himself is described first. After much that Isaiah says about him in such a way that even the Jews themselves are struck dumb, and so as not to take too long by quoting it all, note just this short passage: "He will bear their sins," he says; "therefore he will possess many as his inheritance and will divide the spoils of the strong, because his soul was handed over to death and he was counted among the wicked, and he bore the sins of many and was handed over for our iniquities." Admit that these things were foretold and prophesied so long beforehand about our Lord Jesus Christ. Why, then, was this bridegroom handed over to death? Why was he counted among the wicked? By so great a humbling of his majesty, what did he accomplish, what did he gain? Who is so deaf as not to hear this, who so dull as not to understand it, who so blind as not to see it? "Therefore," he says, "he will possess many as his inheritance and will divide the spoils of the strong, because his soul was handed over to death and he was counted among the wicked." What is this, heretics, that you boast of your small numbers, if our Lord Jesus Christ was handed over to death precisely so that he might possess many as his inheritance? And who are these many, and how widely do they fill the earth? Let us hear what follows.

Now that the bridegroom has been foretold and portrayed, let the bride too come forward in the words of Isaiah. Let us read of her in the truth of the sacred pages and recognize her throughout the world. The apostle Paul too quoted this testimony as a prophecy about the holy Church, so the quarrelsome evasions of the heretics have nowhere to run: "Rejoice, O barren one," he says, "you who do not bear; break forth and shout, you who are not in labour, for the children of the deserted one are more than those of her who has a husband." Where, I ask, is your boasting about your small numbers? Are these not the many of whom it was said a little earlier, "Therefore he will possess many as his inheritance"? For what is his inheritance if not his Church? "The children of the deserted one," he says, "are more than those of her who has a husband", meaning by her who has a husband the synagogue of the Jews, since it had received the Law. From this what we are saying can now be judged. Let these people compare their own multitude, settled among the Africans or in Africa, with the multitude of the Jews, scattered through all the lands wherever they are, and let them see how very few they are by comparison. How then will they claim that it was said of them, "The children of the deserted one are more than those of her who has a husband"? Again, let them compare the multitude of Christians throughout all the nations with which they are not in communion, and see how few all the Jews are by comparison; and let them at long last understand that this prophecy has been fulfilled in the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world: "The children of the deserted one are more than those of her who has a husband." But granted that it may be obscure, a riddle, which woman with a husband this deserted one is preferred to in the number of her children, still, whoever contradicts the claim that this is the Church of Christ, of which it was said, "The children of the deserted one are more than those of her who has a husband," contradicts not me but the apostle.

How she was to have many children, he goes on to say next: "For the Lord has said: Enlarge the place of your tent and of your courts; drive in your stakes, do not hold back; lengthen your cords and strengthen your pegs. Spread out further to the right and to the left. Your offspring will possess the nations, and you will inhabit the deserted cities. Do not fear, for you will prevail; and do not be afraid because you were held in loathing. You will forget your everlasting shame and will no longer remember the disgrace of your widowhood. For I am the Lord who makes you, the Lord is his name; and he who has set you free, the God of Israel, will be called God of the whole earth." See how far she was commanded to stretch out her cords: until her God, the God of Israel, is called God of the whole earth. For of her, and to her, it is said in another place through the same prophet: "For Zion's sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem's sake I will not rest, until my righteousness goes forth like light, and my salvation burns like a torch. All nations will see your righteousness, and kings your glory. He will call you by your new name, which the Lord will name, and you will be a crown of beauty in the sight of the Lord and a royal diadem in the hand of your God. No longer will you be called Forsaken, and your land will no longer be called Deserted. For you will be called My Will, and your land the Whole World." What clearer statement can still be demanded? See how many, how clear are the passages from a single prophet! And yet there is resistance and contradiction, not against any man but against the Spirit of God and the most evident truth. And yet those who want to glory in the Christian name begrudge the glory of Christ himself, refusing to believe that what was foretold of him so long beforehand is being fulfilled, when it is no longer foretold but shown, seen and held in our hands. Indeed, if I wanted to collect into this one letter the testimonies from all the prophets to the Church foreshadowed in them, which we see before us just as we read of it, I fear I would seem myself to judge them few, when they are so many that if I wanted to gather all of them from Isaiah alone, I would exceed the proper length of this work.

Now let us hear a few passages from the Psalms, sung so long beforehand, and let us see them being fulfilled now with great joy. And first, let them hear the very passage that Petilian put in his letter (with what face, I do not know), and let them declare its meaning: "The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession." For what Christian has ever doubted that this was foretold of Christ, or understood this inheritance to be anything other than the Church? And because she was to hold both good and bad within the same nets of the sacraments, he says, "You will rule them with a rod of iron; you will shatter them like a potter's vessel." For by the same firm and unbending justice the good are ruled and the wicked are shattered.

Who has wandered so far from the divine words, and is so out of tune with them, that he does not recognize the gospel itself when that psalm is sung in which it is written: "They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. They looked and stared at me; they divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots"? Indeed, when the evangelist told how this was done, he remembered this testimony. And what was bought by the price of this cross, by such great lowliness of such great loftiness, by that most innocent and divine blood, if not what is said later in the same psalm: "All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight, for the kingdom is the Lord's, and he shall rule over the nations"? Did not the apostle explain that what is written was said of the preachers of the new covenant: "Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world"? Of whom but Christ is this to be understood: "The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and has called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting. Out of Zion comes the beauty of his splendor"? Whose voice but Christ's is this: "I slept, troubled"? And what troubled him follows next: "The sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword." Whose, if not those who shouted, "Crucify him, crucify him"? What was all this for? For whose good, for whose gain? Hear what follows: "Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth." There you have Christ sleeping in his passion and rising above the heavens in his resurrection. And how is his glory over all the earth, if not because his church is over all the earth? In these two very short sentences, you heretics, I put to you the whole question at issue between us. "Be exalted above the heavens, O God," it says, "and let your glory be over all the earth": why do you proclaim the Lord Christ exalted above the heavens, and yet refuse communion with his glory over all the earth?

The seventy-first psalm is titled "For Solomon." But because things are said in it that cannot fit that temporal king, who afterward sinned grievously, they are defended quite unanswerably, even against the Jews themselves, as foretold of Christ. And no Christian denies this, for the things said there are such that no one can doubt they refer to Christ. There, too, things are said in which we may recognize the church spread throughout the whole world, with all kings also made subject to Christ: "And he shall rule," it says, "from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth"—from the river, that is, where the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove and the voice from heaven made him known. Then it goes on: "Before him the Ethiopians shall fall down, and his enemies shall lick the dust; the kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of the Arabians and of Sheba shall bring presents. And all the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him." And a little later: "And in him all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed; all nations shall magnify him. Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wonders, and blessed be the name of his glory for ever and for ages of ages, and the whole earth shall be filled with his glory. So be it, so be it." Go now, Donatists, and shout: "Let it not be, let it not be!" The word of God has defeated you, saying: "So be it, so be it." See, the church spread through the whole world has been made plain in the psalms, the church on which the glory of her king rests. Hence she is also queen, his bride, of whom it is said to him in the forty-fourth psalm: "The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed round with many colors." And at once the divine word turns to exhort her: "Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house, for the king has desired your beauty, for he is your God." Notice how the divine prophecy begins to address the bride of Christ: "Hear, daughter," it says, "and see." But you want neither to hear these things foretold nor to see them fulfilled; and yet you both hear and see them, against your will. Hear, then, what is said to her a little later; hear from the divine page how it is foretold, and see in all the earth how it is fulfilled: "In place of your fathers," it says, "sons are born to you; you will make them princes over all the earth." How many testimonies of Scripture on this matter I am passing over, those who read them know, and so do I; but I do not wish to overload a letter to which I am demanding a reply.

What will they say to these things we have cited from the law, the prophets and the psalms about the church of Christ which is spread throughout the whole world—the church they in their perversity would rather fight against than be corrected and share communion with? What, I ask, will they say? That these things are false, or that they are obscure? But they do not dare to say they are false, for they are crushed by the weight of such great authority. So, while admitting that these things are true, they maintain that they cannot be fulfilled—as if it were anything other than charging a prophecy with falsehood to say that what it foretold cannot come to pass; for that is to say it is not prophecy but rather false prophecy. And when you ask them why these things cannot be fulfilled, they answer: "Because people are unwilling. For man," they say, "was created with free will: if he wills, he believes in Christ; if he does not will, he does not believe. If he wills, he perseveres in what he believes; if he does not will, he does not persevere. And so, when the church had begun to grow throughout the world, people were unwilling to persevere, and the Christian religion failed among all nations except the party of Donatus." As if the Spirit of God did not know the future wills of human beings! Who but a complete madman would say that? Why, then, did he not rather foretell what he knew would come of human wills? For on the view these people take of how these things were foretold, anyone who likes can be a prophet: when what he has predicted does not come true, he can answer, "People were unwilling; for they are Christians by free will." In this way someone could have prophesied that Christ would not suffer on the cross but die by the sword, and then, when it turned out otherwise, answer: "What have I done wrong? People, being endowed with free will, did not want to do to him what I had foretold, and did what they themselves wanted." Who does not see how many things could have been prophesied in this way, or still could be, by anyone at all? For who would doubt that Judas would certainly not have betrayed Christ had he not willed to, and that Peter would not have denied the Lord three times had he not willed to? Yet the prediction about them was certain precisely because God foresees even future wills.

Yet although these things are plain even to slow hearts, let us hear on this matter the voice of the Word himself, uttered by the mouth of his own flesh. Certainly, after his resurrection, when he was offering himself to be touched and handled by the hands of his doubting disciples, and when he had taken in their presence what they had handed him and had eaten it, he said to them: "These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms had to be fulfilled." And of whom but him were those things written which we too have cited from the law, the prophets and the psalms, as I have shown point by point? Since, then, he who is the Truth himself says, "Everything had to be fulfilled," how can these people deny it, unless because they are enemies of the truth? And if they still say these things are obscure, on this point too let us hear the Head himself, the truest revealer of his own body. For when he had said, "Everything written about me in the law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms had to be fulfilled," as though we were asking whether in his words "about me" the church too was to be understood—because of what is written, "The two shall be in one flesh"—so that we might hold firm divine oracles not only about the Head but about the body as well, the evangelist goes on to say: "Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, and he said to them: Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day." Here the Head himself is shown, who also offered himself to be handled by the hands of the disciples. See how he adds something about the body, which is the church, so as not to let us go astray about either the Bridegroom or the bride: "And that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem." What could be truer than these words, what more divine, what plainer? I am ashamed to commend them with words of my own—and are the heretics not ashamed to attack them with words of theirs?

Let them say that the testimonies I have set out from the law, the prophets and the psalms are obscure, spoken figuratively, and capable of being understood in other ways—although even with those I have done all I could to keep them from daring to say even this. But suppose they do say it: is this too spoken obscurely, or veiled in the shadow of a riddle, which Christ himself said: "Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise on the third day, and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem"? If "I slept, troubled" is obscure, is "it was necessary for the Christ to suffer" obscure? If "Be exalted above the heavens, O God" is obscure, is "and to rise on the third day" obscure? Again, if "your glory over all the earth" is obscure, is "and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations" obscure? If "The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and has called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting" is obscure, is "that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations" obscure? For the earth was called from the rising of the sun to its setting in just the way he himself says: "I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." If "Out of Zion comes the beauty of his splendor" is obscure, is "beginning from Jerusalem" obscure? For Zion is the same as Jerusalem. But what is that to me? Let them say that the passages I have set out from the law, the prophets and the psalms have nothing to do with these words of the Lord that are read in the gospel: I do not care, I do not object. Yet certainly, unless this had been foretold in the law, the prophets and the psalms—whether in the testimonies I myself have adduced or in others—the Lord would never have said, "Everything written about me in the law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms must be fulfilled," and then, having opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, taught them the very things written about him in the law, the prophets and the psalms by saying: "Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise on the third day, and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem." I might not have been able to recognize these things as written in the law, the prophets and the psalms; yet he who is the Truth says that this is written there. But even if he had not said that these things were written there, it would undoubtedly have been enough for Christians that Christ himself had said that repentance and the forgiveness of sins must be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. But he wished to strengthen his doubting disciples, even after they had seen and handled his body, with the greater proof of the Scriptures rather than by presenting himself as visible and tangible to mortal senses. Let us hold fast, then, to the church as marked out by the Lord's own mouth: where it was to begin and how far it was to reach—beginning, that is, from Jerusalem and reaching to all nations.

Now if anyone says here that Jerusalem is not to be understood as that visible city but is used figuratively, so as to be taken spiritually as the whole church, eternal in the heavens and in part a pilgrim on earth, he might just as well say that this too was said figuratively: "It was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise on the third day"—and whoever says that is not to be counted a Christian in any sense. So, just as that was meant literally, so too was what was added about the church of all nations beginning from Jerusalem. For the Lord was explaining that these things had been said about him in the law, the prophets and the psalms, and the explanation itself certainly could not have been figurative; otherwise it would not be an explanation. Moreover, if Jerusalem, taken figuratively and understood spiritually, signifies the universal church, how does the universal church begin from the universal church—as though Jerusalem began from Jerusalem? It is clear, then, that this was said literally of that city where the church is shown to have begun, as he himself makes plain again and again, leaving no hiding place for heretical cunning to lie in wait. For he goes on to say: "And you are witnesses of these things, and I am sending my promise upon you; but stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high." In the very city where he ordered them to stay until they were clothed with power from on high—that is, with the Holy Spirit, whom he had promised to send—in that city he foretold the church would begin. And if they do not think it was Jerusalem, let them hear what follows: "Then he led them out as far as Bethany, and he lifted up his hands and blessed them. And it came to pass that, when he had blessed them, he parted from them. And they returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually in the temple praising God." See, here is shown the city in which he ordered them to stay until they were clothed with power from on high.

Here, indeed, it is left unsaid how many days he was with them after he had shown himself alive after his passion to their eyes and hands. But it is not passed over in silence in the Acts of the Apostles, where once again the church that was to spread throughout the world is foretold with the same plainness in the Lord's words. There no one at all is allowed to doubt—unless he doubts the trustworthiness of the holy Scriptures—that it was the visible city of Jerusalem from which the church began after the resurrection and ascension of the Lord Jesus Christ, and that he wished to show nothing other than the places of this earth from which he would give it its beginning, and how he would spread it from there through all lands. For this is what is written in the Acts of the Apostles: "In my first account, O Theophilus, I dealt with all that Jesus began to do and to teach, until the day when he chose the apostles through the Holy Spirit, commanding them to preach the gospel. To them he also showed himself after his passion by many signs, appearing to them over forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. And while he was staying with them, he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for his promise, 'which you have heard,' he said, 'from my mouth: for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit, whom you are also to receive not many days from now.' So when they had come together, they asked him, saying: 'Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?' He answered them: 'It is not for you to know the times which the Father has set by his own authority; but you will receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the whole earth.'" See, here too it is made plain where the church was to begin and how far it was to reach.

What do they say to this, those who most arrogantly call themselves Christians and most openly contradict Christ? We hold this church; against these divine words we admit no human accusations. For we are deeply moved that our Lord, whom it is sacrilegious and impious not to believe, left these wholesome instructions to the early church as his very last words spoken on earth. For having said these things, he soon ascended into heaven; he wished to guard our ears in advance against those whom he had foretold would arise as time went on and say, "Look, here is the Christ! Look, there!"—and he warned us not to believe them. Nor have we any excuse if we believe against the voice of our Shepherd, a voice so clear, so open, so plain that no one, however dull and slow of heart, can say, "I did not understand." For who does not understand: "Thus it was necessary for him to suffer and to rise on the third day, and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem"? Who does not understand: "You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the whole earth. When he had said this he was lifted up, and a cloud took him, and they saw him going into heaven"? What does this mean, I ask you? When the last words of a dying man about to go down to the underworld are heard, no one says that he lied, and an heir who happens to have disregarded them is judged impious. How then shall we escape the wrath of God if, whether by disbelieving or by despising them, we reject the last words of the only Son of God, our Lord and Savior—who was about to go into heaven, who looks down from there to see who neglects those words and who keeps them, and who will come from there to judge all? I have the plainest voice of my Shepherd commending the church to me and describing it without any ambiguity. I shall have only myself to blame if I let myself be led astray and wander from his flock, which is the church itself, through the words of men—especially since he has warned me, saying: "Those who are my sheep hear my voice and follow me." See, his voice is clear and plain. Whoever hears it and does not follow him, how will he dare to call himself one of his sheep? Let no one say to me, "Oh, but what did Donatus say? Oh, what did Parmenian say, or Pontius, or any of them?" For we must not agree even with Catholic bishops if they happen somewhere to be mistaken, so that they hold some opinion contrary to the canonical Scriptures of God. But if they fall into this while keeping the bond of unity and charity, what the apostle says will happen in their case: "And if in anything you think otherwise, God will reveal this too to you." These divine words about the universal church, however, are so plain that none but heretics, with stubborn perversity and blind fury, could bark against them.

But we have shown that the church was foretold in the word of God, its bridegroom, whether through the law, the prophets and the psalms or by his own mouth, as a church that would begin from Jerusalem and reach to the ends of the earth. How it began from Jerusalem and, spreading out from there into all nations, bears fruit is also shown in that same word of God through the apostles. As I have already mentioned, it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that the Lord said: "You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the whole earth." Then it continues: "When he had said this, he was lifted up as they watched, and a cloud took him out of their sight. And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, two men in white clothing suddenly stood beside them. They said: 'Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.' Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a sabbath day's journey away. When they had come in, they went up to the upper room where they were staying: Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James. All these were devoting themselves with one accord to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers. In those days Peter stood up among the disciples and spoke; the crowd of people numbered about a hundred and twenty." Next it tells how, after Peter had spoken, Matthias was put in the place of Judas, who betrayed the Lord. After his ordination the scripture goes on: "When the days of Pentecost were being fulfilled, they were all together in one place. Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. Divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance. Now there were living in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. When this sound came, the crowd gathered and was bewildered, because each of them heard them speaking in his own language. They were astonished and amazed, and said to one another: 'Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? How is it, then, that each of us has heard his own native language? Parthians and Medes and Elamites, Jews living in Mesopotamia and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya around Cyrene, visitors from Rome, both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs: we hear them speaking of the mighty works of God in our own tongues.' They were astonished and perplexed, saying to one another: 'What does this mean?' But others mocked them, saying: 'These men are full of new wine.' Then Peter, standing with the eleven disciples, raised his voice and addressed them: 'Men of Judea and all you who live in Jerusalem, let this be known to you'", and the rest, in which he urges them to faith. When he had finished, the scripture continues the story: "When they heard this, they were cut to the heart and said to Peter and the apostles: 'Brothers, what shall we do? Show us.' Peter said to them: 'Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the grace of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is to us and to our children and to all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God will call.' And with many other words he testified to them, saying: 'Save yourselves from this crooked generation.' Those who accepted this word believed and were baptized, and about three thousand souls were added that day." See how the church began from Jerusalem, and from there it was to go out through every language. This was foreshadowed in those who were gathered there, received the Holy Spirit, and spoke in all languages.

Next let us see how it went out through the other nations, as Peter himself had foretold when he said: "For the promise is to us and to our children and to all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God will call." The narrative goes on in order through what was done at that time in Jerusalem, up to the martyrdom of Stephen the deacon, where Saul is also mentioned as approving of his killing. When that was over, the story continues: "On that day a great persecution arose against the church in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria; the apostles remained in Jerusalem." See how what the Lord had said, step by step, is now fulfilled: "You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the whole earth." It had already happened in Jerusalem. Judea and Samaria came next, because they were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria. For soon afterward it says of them: "Those who had been scattered went through the cities and villages, preaching the word of God." The apostles had also gone, after hearing that Samaria had received the word of God, and the Samaritans received the Holy Spirit through the laying on of their hands. So it is said of Peter and John: "Peter and John, having testified to the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel in many villages of the Samaritans on the way." Next comes the account of the eunuch who was baptized by Philip on his way back from Jerusalem, and of Philip himself it says: "The angel of the Lord caught Philip away from him, and the eunuch saw him no more, but went on his way rejoicing. Philip, however, was found to have come to Azotus, and from there, as he went back, he preached the gospel in all the cities until he came to Caesarea." So we find that the gospel was preached through the cities of Judea and Samaria as well. It remained, then, for it to be preached in due order through all the nations too, as the Lord had said, to the whole earth. So Saul is called from heaven and turned from persecutor into preacher, and the Lord says of him to Ananias: "Go, for he is a chosen vessel of mine, to carry my name before the nations and kings and the children of Israel, to be magnified. For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name's sake." So now we have the church in Jerusalem and throughout all Judea and Samaria, as is said quite plainly a little later: "The churches throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace. They were built up and strengthened in the fear of the Lord, and were filled with the comfort of the Holy Spirit." Then, after a short passage, we come to the place where the centurion Cornelius believed and was baptized with his household, all of them uncircumcised Gentiles. Before this happened, Peter, while praying, was caught up in spirit and saw heaven opened and a kind of vessel, like a clean linen sheet bound by its four corners. In it were every kind of four-footed creature and wild beast and bird of the air. A voice came: "Peter, get up, kill and eat." Peter said: "Lord, I have never eaten anything common and unclean." The voice spoke to him again: "What God has cleansed, you must not call common." We need not guess whether the nations who were to believe were signified by this vision, for the apostle himself explains that this is what was shown to him in that vessel. When he had entered the house where Cornelius was, and many had gathered, he said to them: "You know well how abhorrent it is for a Jewish man to associate with a foreigner or visit him; but God has shown me that I should call no one common or unclean." This is how he explained the voice he had heard about the animals shown in that sheet: "What God has cleansed, you must not call common." Who, then, can fail to see that the vessel signified the whole world with all its nations? That is also why it was bound by four corners: these are the four well-known parts of the world, east and west, south and north, which scripture mentions very often. It would take too long to recount all the places Paul visited after he was sent to the nations, sowing the word of God and strengthening the churches that had sprung up. When the Jews at Antioch opposed him, he and Barnabas said to them: "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first. But since you have rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, we are now turning to the nations. For so the Lord has commanded us: 'I have set you as a light for the nations, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.'" The passage continues: "When the nations heard this, they received the word of God, and as many as had been destined for eternal life believed." See, here too the testimony from the prophet Isaiah is cited, which we also have quoted: that there should be salvation to the ends of the earth.

I will not mention the nations that believed after the time of the apostles and joined the church. Let them tell us only how the churches we find in the holy writings perished through an African sedition: those in the Acts, in the letters of the apostles, and in the Apocalypse of John, which both sides embrace and to which both sides submit. We have received these churches not from the councils of quarrelling bishops, not from newfangled debates, not from the records of courts or town councils, but from the holy canonical writings. How could the church of Antioch, where the disciples were first called Christians, have perished through the crimes of Africans? What African wind could blow so violently as to carry this plague off and scatter it so far, to Athens, Iconium and Lystra? In those places not even the names could be known of those through whom, or about whom, this evil arose. Who destroyed the churches founded by the apostles' labour? At the end of the Letter to the Romans the same apostle, the teacher of the nations, says: "On some points I have written to you rather boldly, by way of reminding you, because of the grace given me by God to be a minister of Christ Jesus among the nations. I serve the gospel of God as a priest, so that the offering of the nations may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to glory before God. For I will not dare to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the nations to obedience, by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Holy Spirit. So from Jerusalem and all around as far as Illyricum I have fully preached the gospel of Christ." Ask, Donatists, if you do not know: ask how many stopping places there are along the overland routes from Jerusalem and all around as far as Illyricum. If we count as many churches, tell us how they could have perished through African quarrels. As for the Corinthians, the Ephesians, the Philippians, the Thessalonians and the Colossians, you keep only the apostle's letters to them, for reading. We keep both the letters, for reading and for faith, and the churches themselves, in communion. Moreover, Galatia is not a single church; there are countless churches in that region. And see how he greeted the Corinthians: "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the church of God that is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia." How many churches do you suppose there are in the whole of Achaia? Perhaps you do not know where Achaia is, and yet you pass judgement on so unknown a province with such blindness that you say it perished through the crimes of Africans. Are not all the places Peter names, Pontus, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, full of flourishing churches? And what of the churches to which John wrote, at Smyrna, Pergamum, Sardis, Thyatira, Philadelphia and Laodicea (Ephesus we have already mentioned)? Let one of you tell me where they are and how far apart they lie. Perhaps you are only now trying to find this out by reading or by hearing. Then find out also how far they are from Africa. And tell us why, with such sacrilegious rashness, you accuse churches entirely unknown to you, which are plainly set forth in the apostolic writings, and why, in such madness, you say they perished through the crimes of Africans. In short, I know what is written about them in the holy canonical books; I do not know what you are saying about them. Certainly, just as we read to you that these are churches of Christ from the books that you also revere, so you must read to us from the books that we also revere how they perished. Or would you have us believe any curses of men, brought from anywhere at all, against churches that are members of the one church spread throughout the whole world, which the Holy Spirit has commended and handed down to us through his scriptures? That is indeed what you would like, but it is not what we would like. Which of us is more justly pleased, you too can see. But you are overcome by stubbornness and do not want to be overcome by the truth. Here are the scriptures of God; here in them are the churches, designated and described both by the universal name of the whole world and by their own names. They did not know what charges your forebears brought against their colleagues; they did not know what sort of judges that case had. How, then, did they perish? Here are the scriptures I believe; here are the churches I am in communion with. Where I read you their names, read me their crimes.

But if you shout or recite from some other source, then after the voice of our shepherd, declared to us most plainly through the mouths of the prophets, through his own mouth, and through the mouths of the evangelists, we do not admit your voice, we do not believe it, we do not accept it. "My sheep," says the heavenly shepherd, "hear my voice and follow me." His voice concerning the church is not obscure. Whoever does not want to stray from his flock, let him hear this voice and follow it. His most faithful steward, the teacher of the nations in faith and truth, through whom Christ himself spoke, says this: "I am amazed that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and turning to another gospel. Not that there is another gospel, but there are some who are troubling you and want to pervert the gospel of Christ. But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel other than the one we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel other than the one you received, let him be accursed." The church has been proclaimed to us as the gospel, a church that was to spread through the whole world. The Lord himself testified that this had been foretold in the law, the prophets and the psalms. He foretold that it would begin from Jerusalem and spread through all nations, and as he was ascending into heaven he announced that his witnesses would be in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the whole earth. Deeds followed these words. The holy scriptures bear witness, step by step, to how it began from Jerusalem, went on into Judea and Samaria, and from there into the whole earth. There the church is still growing, until, by the end, it takes hold of the remaining nations where it is not yet present. Whoever preaches any other gospel, let him be accursed.

But anyone who says that the Church has perished from the rest of the world and has survived only in Africa, in the party of Donatus, is preaching a different gospel. Therefore let him be anathema; or else let him read this to me in the holy Scriptures, and then he will not be anathema.

"I read it," he says. For Enoch alone among all men pleased God and was taken up. Afterwards, when the whole world was destroyed by the flood, Noah alone, with his wife, his sons and his sons' wives, was found worthy to be saved in the ark. They also add the case of Lot, who alone with his daughters was rescued from Sodom, and of Abraham himself, and of Isaac and Jacob, who were few in pleasing God in a land given over to idols and demons.
