Finally, when the people of Israel had multiplied and the kings were reigning in the promised land, which had been divided among all twelve tribes, they recall that ten tribes were split off and handed over to Solomon's servant, while two remained to Solomon's son for the kingdom centred on Jerusalem. "So too now," they say, "the whole world has fallen away, but we have remained in the temple of God, that is, in the Church, like those two tribes." And when very many disciples were following the Lord Jesus Christ, seventy-two fell away and only the twelve remained with him. With these and similar examples the heretics try to make a virtue of their small numbers, and they never stop blaspheming against the multitude of the Church spread throughout the whole world in the saints. But I ask them this: if, God forbid, I refused to believe that these very examples they cite are true, how would they convince me? Would it not be from the holy Scriptures, where they are read so plainly that anyone who accepts those writings in faith cannot help acknowledging these things as entirely true? Now if I am compelled to believe these examples are true because they are written in a place where I cannot say that what is written is false, why do they not believe the same Scriptures about the Church spread throughout the whole world? See, we believe all those things. Let them also believe what the Lord said, that repentance and the forgiveness of sins would be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. Let them believe what he said last of all as he was about to ascend into heaven: "You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the whole earth." Let both those things and these be believed to be true, and no dispute will remain between us, since neither do those truths stand in the way of these, nor these of those. "We do believe these things too," they say, "and we confess that they were fulfilled; but afterwards the world fell away, and only the communion of Donatus remained." Let them read this to us, as they read about Enoch, about Noah, about Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, about those two tribes that were left when the ten were separated, and about the twelve apostles who remained when the rest fell away. Let them read this in the same way, and we will put up no resistance. But if they do not read it from the holy Scriptures, and instead try to persuade us by their own quarrelling, then I believe what is read in the holy Scriptures and I do not believe what is said by empty-headed heretics. And since they think they should be compared with those two tribes that remained with Solomon's son, let them read, and they will regret having made this choice. For this is how the Scriptures speak of the two peoples: the part that was at Jerusalem is called Judah, while the other part, which was separated off in greater numbers with Solomon's servant, is called Israel. Let them read what the prophets say about each, how they call Judah worse than Israel, so much so that they say faithless Israel was justified by the sins of treacherous Judah; that is, the sins of the one were so grave that, compared with her, the other must be called righteous. Yet the sins of neither did any harm to the righteous who are found to have lived both here and there. For even in the part they put forward as an example of perdition, that is, in Israel, there were holy prophets. There was that memorable Elijah, to say nothing of the others, to whom it was even said: "I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal." So that part of the people is by no means to be regarded as a heresy. For God had ordered those tribes to be separated so that the kingdom, not the religion, would be divided, and so that in this way punishment would be inflicted on the kingdom of Judah. God never commands a schism or a heresy to come about. Nor, just because kingdoms throughout the world are often divided, is Christian unity therefore divided, since the Catholic Church is found on both sides.

I thought it worth recalling this about Judah and Israel chiefly so that these people may be reminded that whatever is said against whole peoples on account of the great number of the wicked does no harm to the righteous who live among the ungodly. Then they may stop collecting texts, whether spoken through the prophets, by the Lord's own mouth or by the evangelists, that are found to be directed against the tares or the chaff of the whole world. For the divine word often rebukes the ungodly crowds of the Church, who are not even reckoned as belonging to the Church yet are called hers because of the sacraments they share with the saints (since they have a certain form of godliness while denying its power, as the apostle says: "having the form of godliness but denying its power"), and it rebukes them as though all were like that and not a single good person remained. From this we learn that they are called "all" within their own particular number, that is, all the children of hell, to which God foreknew that they belong. So these people, acting either from ignorance or from deceit, collect from the Scriptures such passages as are found to be said either against the wicked who are mixed with the good until the end, or about the devastation of the former people of the Jews, and they try to twist them against the Church of God, so as to make it seem that she has failed and perished from the whole world. Let them stop bringing forward such things, then, if they mean to reply to this letter. For when we say that the Church is spread throughout the whole world, we do not mean that only the good are in her sacraments and not also the wicked, who are far more numerous, so that the good are few by comparison with them, although considered in themselves the good make up a huge number.

We have countless testimonies both about the mixing of the wicked with the good in the same communion of the sacrament (just as Judas, wicked from the beginning, lived among the eleven good apostles), and about the fewness of the good when compared with the greater number of the wicked, and again about the multitude of the good when considered in itself. Of these, so as not to go on too long, I will mention a few. There is the passage in the Song of Songs which every Christian recognizes as said of the holy Church: "As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters." Why does it call them thorns, if not because of the wickedness of their conduct, and why does it call the same people daughters, if not because of their share in the sacraments? Ezekiel too sees certain people marked so that they would not perish along with the wicked, and of them he is told: "those who groan and grieve over the sins and iniquities of my people that are committed in their midst." He would not call them his people, whom he soon orders to perish, with only those marked ones left unharmed, unless they were the people who bore his sacraments. And the Lord says of the tares sown on top of the wheat: "Let both grow until the harvest," that is, the wheat and the tares; and he himself explains that the harvest is the end of the age and that the field in which both were sown is the world. Both, then, must grow throughout the world until the end of the age. So these people are not permitted to suppose or assert what they say, that all the good have disappeared from the world so as to remain only in the party of Donatus. For they make this attempt against the perfectly plain statement of the Lord, who says, "The field is the world," and, "Let both grow until the harvest," and, "The harvest is the end of the age." There is also another perfectly plain parable about the mixing of good and bad within the same communion and bond of the sacraments, which the Lord himself both tells and explains: "The kingdom of heaven," he says, "is like a net cast into the sea, which gathers fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it up onto the shore, sat down, and chose the best into their vessels, but threw the bad away. So it will be at the end of the age: the angels will come out and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and will throw them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." So no mixture of the wicked frightens the good into wanting to break the nets, as it were, and leave the congregation of unity in order to avoid having to put up with people who do not belong to the kingdom of heaven sharing in the sacraments; for when the net has come to the shore, that is, to the end of the age, the proper separation will be made, not by human rashness but by divine judgment.

As for the fewness of the good, the Lord himself says quite plainly: "Enter through the narrow gate. How wide and broad is the road that leads to destruction, and many are those who travel by it; how narrow is the gate and hard the road that leads to life, and few are those who enter by it." The Donatists think they are these few, and so they say that the world has perished while they themselves have remained in the small number the Lord praised. When they are compared with others in this way, we set against them the Rogatists or the Maximianists, who are far fewer and who separated from them, if they think fewness is something to boast about. But let them read that this fewness was commended by the Lord in comparison with the multitude of the wicked, while the Scriptures have not kept silent about the multitude of the good when considered in itself, and let them see how many testimonies are to be found. Why else is the very seed of Abraham promised to be like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea, if not because of its countless multitude, since the apostle says that "In Isaac shall your seed be called" was said because it is not the children of the flesh but the children of the promise who are counted as seed? Why else are the children of the desolate woman more than those of her who has a husband? Why else will many come from east and west and sit at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, while the children of the kingdom, that is, the ungodly Jews, go into the outer darkness? Why else does the apostle say, "to purify for himself a people abounding, zealous for good works"? Why else does the Apocalypse say that the saints, the children of the Church, are thousands of thousands? See, the very ones who are called few are also called many. Why, unless they are many when considered in themselves but few in comparison with the wicked?

"It was said of us," they say, "'Those who were last will be first.' For the gospel came to Africa later, and that is why it is nowhere written in the apostolic letters that Africa believed. But of the eastern and other nations which the holy books record as having received the Christian faith, it was said, 'Those who were first will be last,' because they were going to fall away from the faith." Is this not the cunning of heretics that we must beware of, people who want to turn God's words away from the truth for which they were spoken to the perversity in which they themselves are? Why should we not rather understand this of the Jews, who became last though they had been first, and of the Christians from the Gentiles, who became first though they had been last? Even if I could not prove this interpretation by some more certain evidence, it ought to be enough for a fair-minded listener that I have found a way out in these words, which makes it clear that they have brought forward nothing in their favour so certain as to be beyond doubt. For even if it were not the Jews and the Gentiles of whom I understood this to be said, several barbarian nations have believed even after Africa, so it is certain that Africa is not last in the order of believing. Besides this, the Lord himself explained of whom he had said this, and shut the mouths of slanderers. For speaking to the Jews, who will say to him, "You taught in our streets," he says: "When you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, but yourselves thrown out. And they will come from east and west and north and south, and will sit at table in the kingdom of God. And see, there are those who are last who will be first, and there are those who are first who will be last." Here, certainly, no grounds for contradiction can be found.

They also say that the Lord's words, "When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?" were spoken about the apostasy of the whole world. We understand this to have been said either because of the very perfection of faith, which is so hard to find among human beings that even in the most admirable saints, such as Moses himself, something is found where they wavered or could have wavered, or else because of that abundance of the wicked and fewness of the good of which we have said enough. That is why the Lord said this as though in doubt. For he did not say, "When the Son of Man comes, he will not find faith on earth," but, "Do you think he will find faith on earth?" It is certainly not fitting for him who knows and foreknows all things to be in doubt about anything; rather, his doubt prefigured our doubt, because human weakness would one day say this on account of the many scandals springing up toward the end of the age. Hence it is said in the Psalms: "My soul has slumbered from weariness; strengthen me in your words." Why "My soul has slumbered from weariness," if not because of what the Lord says: "Because iniquity has abounded, the love of many will grow cold"? And why "strengthen me in your words," if not because of what follows: "But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved"? So there are people throughout the whole world in whom, because iniquity abounds, love will grow cold; and again there are people throughout the whole world who will be saved by persevering to the end, because, he says, "Let both grow until the harvest," and, "The harvest is the end of the age, and the field is the world." To this human weakness also belongs that cry: "Save me, Lord, for the holy one has failed, for truths have dwindled among the children of men." And yet among these there is one heart and one soul of the faithful, directed toward God, crying, "Save me, Lord." For this man who says "Save me, Lord" is one in such a way that he is made up of many; and so a little later in the same psalm it is said: "Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord." And again a little later it is said in the plural: "But you will keep us and guard us from this generation and for ever." What generation, if not the one of which it was said above: "The holy one has failed, and truths have dwindled among the children of men"? But both kinds of people are throughout the whole world until the end, because, he says, "Let both grow until the harvest," and, "The field is the world, the harvest the end of the age." For this one man, who is the body of Christ made up of many, will be taken up like Enoch for pleasing God, and will be rescued like Lot from Sodom and like Noah from the flood. In him are the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, because his soul slumbers from weariness when he asks to be strengthened in the words of God. And in that psalm he says where that weariness comes from: "Weariness," he says, "has seized me because of sinners who forsake your law." He likewise cries out when his heart is in anguish from that same weariness; but let them see where he cries out from: "From the ends of the earth," he says, "I have cried to you, while my heart was in anguish." He truly suffers persecution for righteousness' sake, not only if he suffers bodily torments (for that is not always the case), but because he always suffers, until iniquity passes away, the torments of the heart, when weariness seizes him because of sinners who forsake God's law. For Lot was not free of all persecution in Sodom, even though no one troubled him with bodily punishments while he lived there; yet, as a righteous man dwelling among them, he tormented his righteous soul by seeing and hearing the wicked doings of others. Of this the apostle says: "Indeed, all who want to live godly lives in Christ will suffer persecution." But of those who forsake God's law (of whom that same body of Christ says, "I saw the senseless and I wasted away"), he says: "But evil men and wrongdoers will go from bad to worse, themselves deceived and leading others into error." But both kinds of people are throughout the whole world until the end, because, he says, "Let both grow until the harvest," and the field is the world, the harvest the end of the age.

I am surprised, however, that these people do not pay attention to what they are saying when they cite in their own favour the Lord's words, "When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?" as if Africa were not part of the earth. For if he said this as though he would find faith in no one at all, then either he spoke of some particular land, and it is uncertain which land he meant, or he spoke of the whole earth, and they cannot show how he did not mean Africa. Indeed, let them take care that he did not touch on people like themselves in the words that follow. For when he had said, "Do you think the Son of Man will find faith on earth?" I believe that, since a vain and puffed-up notion could enter the hearts of certain proud heretics who have separated themselves from the unity of the world in some part of the earth, namely that they alone were righteous while the other nations through which the communion of the Church is spread were failing and perishing from the faith, the evangelist immediately went on: "He also told this parable to some who thought themselves righteous and despised others." And there follows the story of the two men praying in the temple, the Pharisee and the tax collector, in whom are figured the proud boasting of good works and the humble confession of sins. So if these people are preparing to reply to this letter, let them stop citing those testimonies which we proclaim together with them, whether against the perdition of the Jews or against the tares, the chaff or the bad fish of the whole world. And just as we have established by the plainest testimonies that the Church is spread throughout the whole world, so let them produce something plain to show that it was foretold that, while the other nations perished from the faith of Christ, Africa alone would remain, together with whatever places bishops from Africa might be sent to.

"It is written," they say, "in the Song of Songs, where the bride, that is, the Church, says to the bridegroom: 'Tell me, you whom my soul has loved, where you pasture your flock, where you lie down at noon.'" This is the only testimony which they think speaks in their favour, because Africa lies in the midday, that is, the southern, part of the world. First, then, I ask how the Church can ask Christ to tell her where the Church is; for there are not two Churches but one. Or else, since they do not deny that it is the Church who says these words to Christ, let them show which is the Church that asks and which is the Church she asks about. For she is seeking where to come to her bridegroom, and says to him: "Tell me, you whom my soul has loved, where you pasture your flock, where you lie down at noon." Already, then, it is the Church who is speaking and asking where she is at noon. For she does not ask, "Where do you pasture, where do you lie down?" and receive the reply, "At noon," as though the bridegroom answered, "I pasture at noon, I lie down at noon"; rather, all these words belong to the question: "Where do you pasture, where do you lie down at noon?" For she goes on speaking: "lest I become like one veiled over the flocks of your companions." Only then does he answer: "Unless you know yourself, O fairest among women," and so on. So these words do not show that the Church is only in the southern region, but that she is established in other parts of the world as well. Perhaps she is asking what belongs to her communion at noon, that is, where her bridegroom pastures and lies down at noon, since he pastures his own and lies down among his own. For some of her members, that is, good believers, come to Africa from lands across the sea, and when they hear that the party of Donatus is here, they are afraid of falling into the hands of some rebaptizer, and so they call upon Christ, praying and saying: "Tell me, you whom my soul has loved, where you pasture your flock, where you lie down at noon"; that is, who make up the noon where you pasture and lie down, meaning those who have love and do not divide unity. And see what she adds: "lest I become like one veiled over the flocks of your companions"; that is, lest, as though hidden, unknown and unrevealed (for that is what "veiled" means), I find myself not over your flock but over the flocks of your companions, who, though at first they were with you, chose to gather outside, not your flock but their own flocks, and did not listen to you when you said, "Whoever does not gather with me scatters," nor to what you said to Peter, "Feed my sheep," not "your sheep." Yet she is not veiled, for she is not under a bushel but on a lampstand, so as to give light to all who are in the house; and of her it was said, "A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden." But to the Donatists she is as good as veiled, for they hear such clear and plain testimonies showing her throughout the whole world, and they prefer to shut their eyes and stumble against the mountain rather than climb it: the mountain which, as a stone cut from a mountain without hands, grew and became a huge mountain and filled the whole earth.

"Where you pasture, where you lie down at noon" can also be understood in another way. For it is the Church's own voice in the Psalms, speaking in the person of Moses the servant of God: "Make your right hand known to me, and those learned in heart in wisdom." It is these people who are called "noon," because of the great light of wisdom and the great heat of love in them. That is why the Spirit of God, urging a certain man to good works through the prophet, also makes him this promise: "And your darkness will be like noon." But even if the words "at noon" had to be understood as some place in the world, the words themselves, as I have said, which all make up a single question, would in no way allow anyone to twist this sentence to suit his own meaning. And even if, as though in answer to a question about where he pastured and where he lay down, the reply "at noon" were given about a place on earth, we would not at once have to take it as Africa. Africa does lie in the southern part of the world, but toward the southwest, not toward the south, where noon truly is. For there the sun makes midday, and under that region of the sky it is rather Egypt that is found. So if the Bridegroom, asked by the bride about some specially beloved place and a private resting place of his own, answered that it was "at noon," the Catholic Church would far more plausibly recognize this in those members of hers who are in Egypt, in the thousands of servants of God who live in holy fellowship throughout the desert, striving to keep the perfection of the gospel precept in which it is said: "Do you wish to be perfect? Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me." How much better could the Son of God be said to pasture and lie down, that is, to rest, there in seclusion, than among the restless mobs of raging Circumcellions, an evil peculiar to Africa! For Isaiah prophesies about Egypt as follows: "On that day there will be an altar to the Lord in the land of the Egyptians and a pillar to the Lord at its border, and it will be a sign to the Lord forever in the land of the Egyptians; for they will cry to the Lord against those who oppressed them, and the Lord will send them a man who will save them; judging, he will preserve them. And the Lord will be known to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians will fear the Lord on that day, and they will offer sacrifices and make vows to the Lord and fulfill them. And the Lord will strike the Egyptians with a plague and heal them in his mercy, and they will turn to the Lord, and he will hear them and heal them." What do they say to this? Why are they not in communion with the church of the Egyptians that was foretold? Or if, by prophetic prefiguration, Egypt stands for the world, why are they not in communion with the Church of the whole world?

So let them search the Scriptures, and against all the many testimonies which show that the Church of Christ is spread throughout the whole world, let them produce even one as certain and as plain as these, to prove that the Church of Christ has perished from the other nations and has remained in Africa alone, as if from another starting point: not from Jerusalem, but from Carthage, where they first set up bishop against bishop. And if we chose to understand Donatus as the prince of Tyre, since Carthage was called Tyrian, what things are prophesied against him through Ezekiel! There he is pointed out above all by what is said to him: "I will show you that you are a man and not God." For these people glory in this man's name more than in God's. And although God alone is without sin, and that Priest who intercedes for us, since of him too it is said, "who is God over all, blessed forever," these imitators of Donatus want so much to appear without sin that they even claim to be the justifiers of men, and claim that their own oil is not the oil of the sinner. It is fitting that it is said to the prince of Tyre: "You have said, 'I am God,' but you are a man and not God." To him it is also said: "Are you better than Daniel?" For Daniel confesses his own sins and the sins of his people. But these men who belong to the prince of Tyre say that they are heard when they pray for the sins of the people precisely because they themselves are without sin. It is fitting that it is said to the prince of Tyre: "Are you better than Daniel?" See, we are able to find something peculiar to them, and that the greatest evil, which arose from the capital of Africa, that is, from Carthage (for people know how aptly Tyre is taken for Carthage); and yet we do not press arguments of this kind. For perhaps Tyre signifies something else. How much more so "noon," since the very words compel a different understanding!

But to see how far they are from being permitted even to look for anything by which to prove it was foretold that, when the other nations fell away from the Christian faith, the Church would remain in Africa alone, let them pay attention to what I have often mentioned: that both grow until the harvest, and that the field is the world and the harvest is the end of the age, as the Lord himself, not we, interpreted his own parable. There is also another very clear point that relieves them entirely of the labor of searching for a way to prove that, the world being lost, the Church has been reduced to the Africans alone. For something can exist and not be found; but something cannot not exist and yet be found. So let them stop looking for what they will be unable to find, not because it is hidden, but because it does not exist. For there are still a number of nations in which the gospel has not yet been preached; yet everything that was foretold about Christ and the Church must be fulfilled. It must therefore be preached among them too, and when that has been fulfilled, then the end will come.

How, then, can these people say that what the Lord said has already been fulfilled, that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem, and that afterward, when all the rest fell away, Africa alone remained to Christ? That prophecy has still to be fulfilled; it has not been fulfilled yet. And when it has been fulfilled, the end will come. For this is what the Lord says: “And this gospel of the kingdom will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come.” How, then, can they claim that the faith had been brought to completion among all nations and that the ruin of all the nations except Africa followed, when the faith has not yet been brought to completion among all nations?

Unless perhaps the only thing left for human madness is to say that the preaching of the gospel among all nations is not being fulfilled from those churches which were founded by the labors of the apostles, but that, those churches having perished, their restoration and the winning of the remaining nations are to come from Africa through the party of Donatus. I think that even they laugh when they hear this; and yet unless they say it, which they blush to say, they have nothing at all to say. But what is that to us? We begrudge no one. Let them read this to us from the holy scriptures, and we will believe. Let them read this to us, I say, from the canon of the divine books: that so many cities which down to the present day have kept the baptism handed on to them by the apostles have fallen away from the faith of Christ because of crimes committed by Africans of which they knew nothing, and must be baptized anew by the party of Donatus, and that from there the gospel must be preached to the other nations which have not yet heard it. Let them read this to us — why do they delay, why do they dodge, why do they stand in the way of the salvation of the nations? — let them read this, and along with that very reading let them send new apostles to rebaptize so many nations and to baptize the rest.

But let them consider carefully, when they come to the Colossians, how they will either read or hear there the letter sent to them, in which the apostle says to them: "We give thanks to God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, praying always for you, since we have heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love which you have for all the saints, because of the hope laid up for you in heaven, of which you heard before in the word of the truth of the gospel, which has come to you, just as in the whole world it is bearing fruit and growing, as it is also among you, from the day you heard and came to know the grace of God in truth." These words agree with the gospel, where it is said: "The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field"; and afterwards the field is explained to be this world. For just as it was foretold that what was sown would grow from the time it was sown until the harvest, so too the apostle says: "in the whole world it is bearing fruit and growing, as it is also among you, from the day you heard." And it grows until the end, because it grows until the harvest; for the harvest is the end of the age. So not only the Colossians, to whom this letter was sent, but also all the others among whom it is read — where the apostle's letter establishes that the good seed was sown and had already then begun to grow and bear fruit — will say: "What new thing are you bringing us? Must the good seed be sown again, when from the time it was sown it grows until the harvest?" If you say that what was sown by the apostles in those places has perished, and that it must therefore be sown again from Africa, the answer will be: "Read this to us from the divine oracles." And that you certainly cannot read, unless you first show that what is written is false, namely that the seed sown there earlier grows until the harvest. And since the divine words in no way contradict one another, you will in no way find in them anything you could cite against so plain a statement. It remains, then, that you are saying these things not from the divine books but from yourselves. Therefore the most fitting answer will be: "Let you be anathema." For the churches founded by apostolic labor hold fast to how carefully they were forewarned: "If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than what you have received, let him be anathema."

Since, then, the church is plainly recognized in the holy scriptures as beginning from Jerusalem and growing through the other nations until it fills them all, to the end of the age — and since not only its grain but also its refuse is mentioned — first be corrected and enter into communion with the grain, and then you will see what you ought to call tares or chaff among them. Otherwise you are driven by a detestable error both to adorn the wicked with the praises due to the good and to charge the good with the crimes of the wicked. For indeed we carry in our hands the documents by which we prove that your forebears, whose schism you follow, handed over the holy books to the flames, as the municipal records show, and could not deny it in the church records; and that these same men were among the judges who passed sentence at Carthage against Caecilian and his colleagues in their absence. Indeed the same men are found in both the municipal and the church records to have been traitors who hand over the scriptures, and are afterwards put forward by you as the condemners of absent traitors. Indeed Nundinarius, who was your deacon at that time, laid bare before Zenophilus the consular all the market-dealings of Lucilla, who bought from the bishops the condemnation of Caecilian, he having become her enemy by preaching the truth. Indeed these same men afterwards sent a letter to the emperor Constantine, and when he had given them bishops as arbiters, as they had requested, they would not accept their verdict; later they accused those same bishops before him as unjust judges, and from others given them at Arles they appealed to the emperor himself; and when he heard the parties, they were found to be slanderers and were condemned, yet they persisted in the same stubborn fury. Indeed you yourselves, who say that Christian holiness has been utterly wiped out from so many nations in which the apostles left it most firmly founded, because they held communion with those whom your forebears had condemned in the council of seventy bishops at Carthage — are you not now in communion with those whom you, three hundred and ten of you, condemned along with Maximian at the Council of Bagai? Is it not on record that Praetextatus of Assuras was condemned in that very council and was accused and attacked by you in the proconsular proceedings, and yet was received back in the very rank in which he had been condemned and died in your communion? Was not Felicianus of Musti, in the same way, in the same case and at the same council, condemned by the bishops and accused before the judges, then afterwards received back by you, and is he not now living among you as a bishop? Are not those who were baptized by these condemned men now in communion with you in that same baptism? But, of course, so many churches overseas founded by apostolic labor lose their salvation and their Christian faith if they have shared the sacraments with men whom they themselves never condemned, since they were never accused before them, and whom they heard had afterwards been cleared and acquitted by others; while the party of Donatus condemns whomever it pleases, and in that very condemnation so magnifies the sacrilege of their schism that it does not hesitate to compare them to those whom the earth swallowed alive — and then, when it pleases, receives them back in the same rank, holds communion with them, and remains holy and unblemished! O rule of Numidian law! O privileges of Bagai! The baptism of Christ is blown upon in contempt in those who received it in the apostolic churches, but in those whom Praetextatus and Felicianus — "condemned sacrilegious men," as the Council of Bagai put it in writing — had baptized, the baptism of Christ is spared: not because it is the baptism of Christ, but because it was given by men who earned the privilege of leaving their condemners as bishops and returning to their condemners as bishops.

Indeed all these things I have been recounting for some time now we cite as recorded in imperial letters and in church, municipal, and proconsular proceedings. And yet, Donatists, if you held the church spread throughout the whole world, which is marked out and portrayed by the clearest testimonies of the canonical scriptures, none of all this ought to count against you at all. For if you were the wheat within it, the crimes of the chaff would not prejudice your case; and if you were the chaff and the crimes were yours, you would in no way prejudice the wheat of the Lord's crop, which has been sown in the Lord's field so as to grow until the harvest — that is, sown in the world so as to grow until the end of the age. In the same way, then, if perhaps you could bring such documents against our chaff — which you have never yet proved to us — and we did not have against you all these weighty things I have mentioned, even so nothing whatever that you might say against their chaff, however true, however manifest, however thoroughly proved, would prejudice our grain spread throughout the whole world. So let all delaying evasions be set aside. Whatever false charge is brought about the sins of men, let conscience be consulted and let it not be raised. Whatever charge about the sins of men is true but either cannot be proved, or could not be proved when it ought to have been, let it not be raised. Whatever charge about the sins of men is both true and proved, yet concerns not the grain hidden among the chaff but the chaff itself, which will be separated at the end, let it not be raised. For we too could raise such charges far more abundantly and convincingly — not with the emptiness with which they do it, so as to rest our case on them, but to show them that we refuse to rely on such things not because we cannot find such things to say, but so as not to waste on unnecessary matters time that is useful for necessary ones. They do it because they cannot find documents, strong and firmly grounded in truth, with which to defend their case, and they want to seem to be saying something, since they blush to keep silent and do not blush to talk emptily. So, setting all such things aside, let them show their church, if they can — not in the talk and rumors of Africans, not in the councils of their bishops, not in the writings of any disputants whatever, not in deceptive signs and wonders, since against these too we have been prepared and put on guard by the word of the Lord — but in the precepts of the law, in the predictions of the prophets, in the songs of the psalms, in the words of the one Shepherd himself, in the preaching and labors of the evangelists, that is, in all the canonical authorities of the holy books. Nor let them do it by gathering and citing things that were said obscurely or ambiguously or figuratively, which anyone may interpret as he pleases according to his own mind. For such things cannot be rightly understood and explained unless those things which have been said most plainly are first held with firm faith.

Whoever, then, is preparing to answer this letter, I warn him in advance not to say to me: "Those men handed over the Lord's books to the flames, those men sacrificed to the idols of the heathen, those men waged a most unjust persecution against us, and you consented with them in everything." For I answer briefly what I have often answered: "Either what you say is false, or, if it is true, the things you speak of concern not the grain of Christ but its chaff." The church does not perish because of these things; at the last judgment it will be winnowed and cleansed by the separating out of all such men. What I am asking about is the church itself: where is the church which, by hearing the words of Christ and doing them, builds on the rock, and which, hearing and doing, bears with those who, hearing and not doing, build on the sand? Where is the wheat that grows among the tares until the harvest — not what the tares themselves have done or are doing? Where is Christ's beloved in the midst of wicked daughters, like a lily among thorns — not what the thorns themselves have done or are doing? Where are the good fish which, until they reach the shore, bear with the bad fish caught in the same net — not what the bad fish themselves have done or are doing?

So, leaving aside these snares of delay, let him show that the church, when so many nations had been lost, was to be preserved in Africa alone, or that from Africa it was to be restored and filled out among all nations. And let him show it without saying: "It is true because I say so, or because that colleague of mine said so, or those colleagues of mine, or those bishops or clergy or laity of ours"; or: "It is true because Donatus, or Pontius, or anyone else, worked this or that miracle"; or: "because people pray at the shrines of our dead and are heard"; or: "because this or that happens there"; or: "because that brother of ours, or that sister of ours, saw such a vision while awake, or dreamed such a dream while asleep." Away with these things, whether they are the fictions of lying men or the portents of deceiving spirits. For either the things reported are not true, or, if some wonders have been done by heretics, we ought to be all the more on our guard. For when the Lord had said that certain deceivers would come who by working signs would deceive even the elect, if that were possible, he added a strong warning, saying: "See, I have told you beforehand." Hence the apostle too warns us, saying: "Now the Spirit says plainly that in the last times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits and doctrines of demons." Moreover, if someone praying at the shrines of heretics is heard, he receives what he receives, whether good or evil, not because of the merit of the place but because of the merit of his own desire. For, as it is written, "the Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world," and "the jealous ear hears all things." And many are heard when God is angry — of such the apostle says, "God gave them up to the lusts of their hearts" — and to many, when he is gracious, God does not grant what they want, so that he may grant what is good for them. Hence the same apostle, speaking of the thorn in his flesh, the angel of Satan which he says was given him to buffet him lest he be exalted by the greatness of the revelations, says: "For this I asked the Lord three times to take it away from me, and he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you; power is made perfect in weakness." Do we not read that some were heard by the Lord God himself on the high places of the mountains of Judea, and yet those high places so displeased God that the kings who did not overthrow them were blamed and those who overthrew them were praised? From this it is understood that the disposition of the one asking counts for more than the place of the asking. As for deceptive visions, let them read what is written: both that Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light, and that dreams have led many astray. Let them also listen to what the pagans tell of marvels done or seen in their temples and with their gods; and yet "the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens." So many people are heard, and in many ways — not only Catholic Christians, but also pagans and Jews and heretics given over to various errors and superstitions. They are heard either by seducing spirits, who nevertheless do nothing unless they are permitted, God judging in a lofty and ineffable way what is to be granted to each; or by God himself, whether as a punishment for wickedness, or as a comfort in misery, or as an admonition to seek eternal salvation. But no one attains to that salvation and eternal life except one who has Christ as his head. And no one can have Christ as head except one who is in his body, which is the church — and that church, like the head himself, we must recognize in the holy canonical scriptures, not search for it in the various rumors and opinions and deeds and sayings and visions of men.

Let no one who is preparing to answer me, then, set such things against me. For I myself do not say that I should be believed that the communion of Donatus is not the church of Christ because certain men who were bishops among them are convicted by church, municipal, and judicial records of having handed over the divine documents to the flames; or because they did not win their case in the episcopal hearing they had requested from the emperor; or because, when they appealed to the emperor himself, they earned a sentence against them from him as well; or because such are the leaders of the circumcellions among them; or because the circumcellions commit such great crimes; or because there are those among them who hurl themselves over cliffs or throw themselves into fires they have kindled for themselves, or who, by terrorizing people, extort their own slaughter even from the unwilling, and seek so many self-chosen and frenzied deaths in order to be venerated by men; or because at their tombs drunken gangs of vagabond men and women, mingled together in wickedness, bury themselves in wine day and night and defile themselves with shameful deeds. Let all this crowd be their chaff, and let it not prejudice the grain, if they themselves hold the church. But whether they hold the church, let them show only from the canonical books of the divine scriptures. For neither do we say that we ought to be believed that we are in the church of Christ because the church we hold has been commended by Optatus of Milevis or Ambrose of Milan or countless other bishops of our communion; or because it has been proclaimed by the councils of our colleagues; or because throughout the whole world, in the holy places frequented by our communion, so many wonders of answered prayers and of healings take place — so that the bodies of martyrs, hidden for so many years, were revealed to Ambrose, as those who ask can hear from many, and at those very bodies a man blind for many years and very well known to the city of Milan received back his eyes and his sight; or because one man saw a dream and another, caught up in the spirit, heard a voice, either telling him not to go over to the party of Donatus or telling him to leave the party of Donatus. Whatever things of this kind happen in the Catholic Church are to be approved because they happen in the Catholic Church; the Catholic Church is not shown to be what it is because these things happen in it. The Lord Jesus himself, when he had risen from the dead and offered his body to the eyes of the disciples to be seen and to their hands to be touched, nevertheless, lest they think they were suffering some deception, judged that they should rather be strengthened by the testimonies of the law and the prophets and the psalms, showing them that the things foretold so long before had been fulfilled in him. So too he commended his church, saying that repentance and forgiveness of sins were to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. He himself testified that this was written in the law and the prophets and the psalms; this we hold as commended by his own mouth. These are the proofs of our case; these are its foundations; these are its supports.

We read in the Acts of the Apostles that it was said of certain believers that they searched the scriptures daily to see whether these things were so. What scriptures, surely, but the canonical scriptures of the law and the prophets? To these have been added the Gospels, the apostolic letters, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Revelation of John. Search all of these and bring out something plain by which you can show either that the church has remained in Africa alone, or that it is from Africa that what the Lord says is to be fulfilled: "This gospel will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come." But bring forward something that needs no interpreter, and not something about which you can be convicted that it was said of another matter and that you are trying to twist it to your own meaning. For you see how that one text you are accustomed to bring forward — "Where do you pasture, where do you lie down at noon?" — when all the words of that passage are examined, points to something far different from what you think; and even if it meant what you want, the Maximianists would beat you on it. For the province of Byzacena and Tripolitania, where they are, whoever they are, are more truly the South than Numidia, where you are strongest. So they can boast of the South more genuinely and more distinctly, and you could not exclude them from this text unless you held to the true and Catholic sense of those words, showing them that, according to the four quarters of the world, the South is reckoned from the south wind rather than from the southwest wind, but that according to the figurative language of the scriptures, "noon" signifies the perfect enlightenment of the mind and the greatest fervor of charity, as it is written: "And your darkness will be like the noonday." So bring forward something that cannot be more truly interpreted against you, but which needs no interpreter at all. Just as this needs no interpreter: "In your seed all nations shall be blessed," because it is not I but the apostle who interprets the seed of Abraham as Christ. Just as this needs no interpreter: "For you shall be called My Delight, and your land the whole world," because it is said to one whom no Christian understands to be anything but the church of Christ. Just as this needs no interpreter: "All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him, for the kingdom is his, and he shall rule over the nations," because it is said in that psalm in which the Lord's passion is set forth, as the gospel also testifies. Just as this needs no interpreter: "That the Christ had to suffer and rise on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem." Just as this needs no interpreter: "And you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the whole earth" — for the subsequent events, established by canonical records, testify that the church began from Jerusalem and from there went out through Judea and Samaria and the other nations. Just as this needs no interpreter: "And this gospel will be preached as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come" — for when the Lord was asked about the end of this age, after speaking of certain beginnings of birth pains, he said, "But the end is not yet," and he foretold that the end would come after the preaching of the gospel throughout the whole world among all nations. Just as this needs no interpreter: "Let both grow until the harvest," because when it did need an interpreter, the Lord himself interpreted it, and he whom no one can contradict explained it himself — above all in that parable which he told, where he himself says that the good seed is the children of the kingdom, the field is the world, and the harvest is the end of the age. Bring forward something like this, even a single text, in which Africa is declared most plainly either to have been left alone while the rest perished, or to have been kept alone as the starting point for renewing and filling the world. For what was soon to perish would not have been commended by so many testimonies, while silence was kept about the one thing that alone was to be left, or from which alone the whole was to be restored and filled. But if you cannot show what we so justly demand of you, yield to the truth, fall silent, be still, and awake from your madness to salvation.

Or do you still say: “If the church is with you, why do you persecute us to drive us into its peace? Or if we are wicked, why do you go looking for us? And if we are tares, let us grow until the harvest”? As if we were doing anything, by whatever means we can, except trying to keep the wheat from being uprooted along with the tares while they are separated before their time. For all who will be good for eternity, even if they are wicked before that time, are not tares but wheat in the foreknowledge of God. And you accuse us by asking why we seek you if you are wicked, as though it were not precisely by being wicked that you have perished. That is why you must be sought: because you have perished. Being lost, you are to be sought; being sought, you are to be found; being found, you are to be called back, like the sheep by the shepherd, like the drachma by the woman, like the son who was dead and came to life again, was lost and is found. For the one who seeks you is he who dwells in the saints and commands that you be sought.

As for persecution, your complaint will die down if you first consider and understand that not all persecution is blameworthy. Otherwise it would not be said in praise: “Whoever secretly slanders his neighbor, him I persecuted.” Every day we see a son complain of his father as if he were his persecutor, a wife of her husband, a slave of his master, a tenant of the landowner, a defendant of the judge, a soldier or a provincial of his commander or king. Very often these people use the most properly ordered authority to restrain and check those subject to them from graver evils by fear of light penalties, though often they also use threats and cruelty to frighten them away from a good life and good deeds. When they restrain people from what is evil and unlawful, they are correctors and counselors; but when they restrain them from what is good and lawful, they are persecutors and oppressors. Even those who restrain people from evil are blamed if the measure of coercion exceeds the measure of the sin. Likewise those deserve blame who rush in a lawless and disorderly way to coerce people who are not subject to them by any law.

So we rightly condemn the lawless outrages and arrogant madness of your Circumcellions, even when they use violence against some very wicked people, because it is not good to punish unlawful acts unlawfully or to deter people from unlawful acts by unlawful means. And when they also persecute innocent people, either without investigating the case or out of the most unjust hatred, who would not shudder at their utterly criminal banditry? But when you thought that the fury of the Maximianists should be curbed by the public laws, so that you could drive them out of the basilicas they held by means of judges' orders, the enforcement of officials, and the help of the towns, and so force them to consider their crime, we do not blame you for that, except that you attacked in them what you yourselves had done. Indeed, what they did was much less serious than what you did. They set up the altar of sacrilegious dissension against the party of Donatus, but you set it up against the whole world, and against the words of him who commended his church as beginning from Jerusalem and spreading through all nations. Moreover, if the Maximianists had dared to resist unlawfully and furiously the orders of the judges that you had obtained against them, would they not have brought judgment on themselves? For the apostle says: “Whoever resists authority resists the ordinance of God, and those who resist bring judgment on themselves. For rulers are not a terror to good work but to evil.” Their work was evil, and you were trying to restrain it through the authorities properly established. If, for the sake of that evil work, they had chosen to oppose the laws by a still worse work, would they not have suffered whatever harm befell them at their own hands and not at yours? In the same way, if anyone had chosen to speak blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego and had been destroyed with his household according to the king's edict, would he have suffered that well-deserved punishment from those three men, after whose deliverance from the fire the king, deeply moved, issued that edict, or even from the king himself, and not rather from himself? And if those forty Jews who had sworn to kill Paul had attacked the armed men by whom Paul was being escorted under lawful protection, would Paul have destroyed them, and not they themselves by resisting the authorities?

Therefore you too, without agitation of mind, without turbulent quarreling, without the bitterness of hatred, should consider carefully the measures that the kings of our communion are enacting against you, and ask for what cause you are suffering. If you find that you are in the church of Christ, rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven. Then you are being crowned as martyrs, and they are judged as persecutors of martyrs. But suppose the holy and canonical scripture proves that you have set up an altar against the church of Christ, that you have been cut off by sacrilegious schism from the Christian unity that is spread throughout the whole world, and that you oppose the body of Christ, which is the church spread throughout the whole world, by rebaptizing, by blaspheming, and by attacking it as far as you can. Then you are impious and sacrilegious. And those who decree that you are to be deterred and restrained from so great a crime so lightly, by the warnings of material losses, the loss of places or of honors or of money, so that you may think about why you are suffering these things, recognize your sacrilege and flee from it, and be freed from eternal damnation, are counted as most diligent rulers and most devout counselors. Catholic Christian emperors owe you this love: that out of Christian gentleness they do not decree that your sacrileges be punished as they deserve, and that out of Christian concern they do not leave them wholly unpunished. God is at work in them in this, and you will not recognize his mercy even in these troubles you complain about. As for us, as far as it lies with us, as far as the Lord grants and permits, we do not set in motion even these laws of very mild coercion against you except for one purpose. We want the Catholic Church to be kept free from your terrors, for the sake of the weakness of the infirm, so that they may be free to choose without fear what to hold and follow. Then, if any of your people commit violence against ours, you, whom we hold like hostages on the estates and in the towns, will not suffer the kind of things your people do, but, being subject to the laws, you will be punished with a fine through properly constituted courts. If this seems hard to you, let your people spare you and keep quiet. But if those who are under you or with you rage against you by refusing to keep quiet, you have no grounds to complain about us. We have placed it in your power, or in that of your people, that you suffer no penalties even while following your heresy, provided the Catholic Church suffers no violence from you or from yours. And if some acts of violence are committed against your will and you are unable to stop them, these very penalties warn you, both mercifully and justly, what kind of people you have among you, people by whom you do not think yourselves defiled. From this you are forced to understand how empty are the slanders you bring against the church of Christ spread throughout the whole world. Then you will no longer reproach us with persecuting you, but rather your own people, if they would rather harass us with their violence and have you crushed by the public laws than calm down from their usual fury. If you do in fact suffer anything hateful and harmful at the hands of our people, who do not keep the measure and the aim of Christian love, I would be quick to say that they are not ours. Either they will become ours if they correct themselves, or they will be separated at the end if they persist in their wickedness. Yet we do not break the nets because of the bad fish, nor do we abandon the great house because of the vessels made for dishonor. And if you too say, by the same rule, that those who inflict such things on the Catholic Church are not yours, prove your intention, correct your error, embrace the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. For if they do not defile you and these others do not defile us, let us not slander one another over crimes that belong to others. Let us grow as grain in one love, and bear with the chaff together until the winnowing.

So then, the testimonies of the canonical scriptures that commend the church as existing in the communion of the whole world need no interpreter, and you can find no such support in those same books for your separation, confined as it is to Africa. Nor do you have any just complaint about persecutions. The church itself endures heavier persecutions the more widely it spreads, and in faith, hope and love it bears everything: not only the kind of things that your Circumcellions and others like them inflict on its members wherever they can, but all the scandals of every kind of wickedness that swarm throughout the whole world, of which the Lord cried out: “Woe to the world because of scandals!” For a son persecutes his father more grievously by living wickedly than a father persecutes his son by chastising him. The slave woman persecuted Sarah more grievously by her wicked arrogance than Sarah persecuted her by due discipline. And those of whom it was said, “Zeal for your house has consumed me,” persecuted the Lord more grievously than he persecuted them when he overturned their tables and drove them out of the temple with a whip.

What more do you have to say? Shall we now bring out that last argument of yours? “Look,” they say, “you hold the church. How will you receive us if we want to come over to you?” I answer briefly: “We receive you in the way the church we find in the holy canonical books receives people.” If you lay aside the passion for contradiction that swells in all who refuse to be overcome by the truth of God and are overcome by their own perversity instead, you can easily understand that the divine sacraments are found both in the good and in the wicked: in the good for salvation, in the wicked for damnation. And though there is so great a difference between those who handle them worthily and those who handle them unworthily, the sacraments themselves are the same, effective for the one to reward and for the other to judgment.

So when the Lord was baptizing more people than John, as is written in the gospel, where the evangelist adds, “although he himself did not baptize, but his disciples,” there was a great difference between Peter and Judas, and yet there was no difference between the baptism given through Peter and that given through Judas. What was given through them was one, though they themselves were not one; it was Christ's, while of the two men one belonged to the members of Christ and the other to the party of the devil. John the Baptist and Paul the apostle, on the other hand, were one, since each was a friend of the bridegroom. Yet because the baptism given by John and the baptism given by Paul were not one, Paul ordered those who had been baptized with the baptism of John to be baptized with the baptism of Christ. And so that baptism was called the baptism of John, but the baptism given through Paul was not called the baptism of Paul. Instead scripture says: “He ordered them to be baptized in Christ.” See: John and Paul are one, and they do not give one thing; Peter and Judas are not one, and they give one thing; but Peter and Paul are one and give one thing. Abraham and Cornelius, both justified by faith, are one, and they did not receive one sacrament. Likewise Cornelius and Simon the magician are not one, and they received one sacrament. But Cornelius and the eunuch whom Philip baptized on the road are one and received one sacrament. So when the sacrament is one, neither different ministers nor different recipients can make what is one cease to be one.

But these people, in wanting what belongs to Christ to belong to men, try to persuade us of utterly false and absurd things, so that there would be almost as many baptisms as there are men through whom baptism is given. So the Lord's words about a man and a man's works, “A good tree bears good fruit and a bad tree bears bad fruit,” they try to twist to mean that someone baptized by a good man is good and someone baptized by a bad man is bad. It follows, whether they like it or not, that someone baptized by a better man is better and someone baptized by a lesser man is lesser. From this it would follow that those whom Jesus himself did not baptize before the Lord's passion, but his disciples did, would have been born again far more holily if they had been baptized by him. For who could even imagine how great the difference was between him and the disciples who baptized them? Did he then begrudge them a holier birth, since he preferred to have them baptized by his disciples while he himself was here? Anyone who believes that is certainly insane. What, then, did the Lord deign to show by this, if not that what was given was his, no matter through whom it was given, and that it was he himself who baptized? Of him the friend of the bridegroom had said, “This is the one who baptizes,” whatever minister's hands baptized the one who believed in him. Paul also says: “I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one may say that I baptized in my own name.” Are we to believe that he too begrudged people a better sanctification, if those baptized by him could have been baptized better in proportion as he was better? Not at all. The intention of this most careful and faithful steward watched for this very thing: that no one should think himself more holily baptized because he was baptized by a holier minister, and so credit to the servant what belonged to the Lord.

Both the good and the wicked, then, give and receive the sacrament of baptism, yet only the good, being spiritually reborn, are built up into the body and members of Christ. So that church to which it is said, “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters,” is certainly among the good. For it is among those who build on the rock, that is, who hear the words of Christ and do them, since he said to Peter when Peter confessed him as Christ, the Son of God: “And on this rock I will build my church.” It is not, therefore, among those who build on sand, that is, who hear the words of Christ and do not do them. For he himself said: “Whoever hears these words of mine and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who builds his house on the rock.” And a little later in the same place he says: “Whoever hears these words of mine and does not do them, I will liken him to a foolish man who builds his house on sand.” Those, then, who by the bond of love are built into the building founded on the rock and into the lily shining white among the thorns will certainly possess the kingdom of God. But as for those who build on sand or are counted among the thorns, who would doubt that they will not possess the kingdom of God? The sacrament of baptism does such people no good at all. And yet, because of their unstable foundation and barren wickedness, no injury should be done even to the sacrament they have.

So then, without the zeal of quarreling, look at that passage in the letter the apostle Paul wrote to the Galatians, and see how right it is that when heretics correct their error, if they have this sacrament as they ought to have had it, they should receive what they lacked, while what they already had should not be condemned and blasphemed. He says: “The works of the flesh are plain: they are fornication, impurity, licentiousness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, anger, dissensions, heresies, envy, drunkenness, carousing, and the like. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God.” None of these people, then, are in the lily or on the rock, and heretics have been placed among them. Why, then, to pass over the rest, do you not baptize again after drunkards, the licentious and the envious? They will not possess the kingdom of God, and so they are not on the rock; and because they are not on the rock, they are certainly not counted as being in the church, since he says, “On this rock I will build my church.” Yet you want us to baptize again after heretics, who are listed among those same thorns that will not possess the kingdom of God, and in whom the sacraments likewise are present. They are the same sacraments, but they do them no good, because although the sacraments are right, the people themselves are perverse.

If you weigh and ponder these things without obstinacy, you can easily understand that in each person what is wrong must be corrected and what is right must be approved, that what is lacking must be given and what is present must be acknowledged. So when a heretic comes to become a Catholic, let him correct his own error, let him not violate Christ's sacrament, and let him receive the bond of peace that he did not have. Without it the baptism he had could not benefit him, for both are necessary for obtaining the kingdom of God: baptism and righteousness. There can be no righteousness in someone who despises the baptism of Christ, but baptism can be present even in someone who does not have righteousness, though it cannot benefit him. For just as the Truth said, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven,” so the same Truth said, “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” Thus not baptism alone but righteousness as well leads to the kingdom, and whoever lacks both, or either one, cannot reach it. So when heretics are told, “You lack righteousness, which no one can have without love and the bond of peace,” and when they themselves admit that many have baptism and do not have righteousness (and if they do not admit it, the divine scripture refutes them), I am amazed at how they think that because we refuse to baptize again those who have a baptism that is not their own but Christ's, we are acting as if we judged that they lacked nothing. And because the baptism they are found to have already is not given to them in the Catholic Church, they suppose they receive nothing there, when in fact they receive there the thing without which what they already have works for their destruction, not for their salvation. But if they will not understand this, it is enough for us that we hold the church which is shown by the clearest testimonies of the holy and canonical scriptures.

Now let the heretic say to me: “How do you receive me?” I answer at once: “As the church receives you to which Christ bears witness. Can you know better how you should be received than our Savior, the physician of your wound?” Here perhaps you say: “Then read me how Christ commanded that those who want to come over from the heretics to the church should be received.” Neither you nor I read that openly and plainly. If John had been a heretic and had baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and Paul had ordered people to be baptized after his baptism, you would win your point so completely that I would have nothing to say against it. On the other hand, if Peter, to whom the Lord said, “He who has been washed once has no need to be washed again,” had been baptized by heretics in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, I would win my point so completely that you would have nothing to say against it. As it is, since we do not find in the scriptures that anyone came over to the church from the heretics and was received either as I say or as you say, I think that if there had been some wise man to whom the Lord Christ bore witness, and we had consulted him on this question, we ought not to hesitate in the least to do what he said, so as not to be judged to be fighting not so much against him as against the Lord Christ, by whose testimony he was commended. Now Christ bears witness to his church. Look, read the gospel where he says: “It was necessary for the Christ to suffer and rise on the third day, and for repentance and forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.” So, setting aside all evasions and shifts, you are to be received in the way this church, spread through all nations, beginning from Jerusalem, receives people. If you refuse, you are not resisting me or any other man who wants to receive you in this way. You are resisting, to your own utter ruin and against your own salvation, the Savior himself, since you refuse to believe that you should be received in the way that church receives people which is commended by the testimony of the one whom you admit it is wicked not to believe.

“But Jeremiah said: ‘It has become to me like lying water that has no faithfulness.’” He did not say this about the water you think he meant. Read carefully. In the manner of the prophets, who customarily speak figuratively, he called the multitude of lying men itself “lying water,” just as we know that in the Apocalypse peoples are called by the name of waters. For this is what Jeremiah says: “Why do those who grieve me prevail? My wound is severe; how shall I be healed? It has become to me like lying water that has no faithfulness.” He said that his wound had become to him like lying water, and by that wound of his he meant those who were grieving him. What he called “those who grieve me” he afterward called “my wound,” and what he said above, “they prevail,” he afterward expressed as “is severe.”

You do the same with the passage where it is written: "Keep away from strange water, and do not drink from a strange spring." You think this was said of the baptism found among heretics, so that it is strange water because heretics will not possess the kingdom of God. As if the same were not true of drunkards, the envious and others of that kind, of whom it is equally said, "They will not possess the kingdom of God"! And yet in all such people, if they have been baptized according to the gospel, the baptism is Christ's, not theirs. So that water is not strange, even though they themselves are strangers, to whom he will say, "I do not know you." Why, then, should I not rather understand the strange water and the strange spring to be the teaching of the evil spirit? By that teaching those who are estranged from God are deceived and led astray, through the ignorance that is in them because of the blindness of their hearts. The apostle commends this point more explicitly: "Now the Spirit says plainly that in the last times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits and doctrines of demons." This is the strange water and the strange spring. For if water in a good sense can be understood as the Holy Spirit, why should water in a bad sense not be understood as the evil spirit? When scripture names water, it does not always mean us to understand this visible sacrament of baptism, but sometimes that and sometimes something else. The Lord's disciples had already baptized others with this visible baptism before the Holy Spirit came upon them according to his promise. Yet of that Spirit the same Jesus says: "If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink. Whoever believes in me, as scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from within him." And the evangelist goes on to explain what this referred to: "This," he says, "he said of the Spirit, which those who believed in him were to receive; for the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified." See, he calls water the Spirit which had not yet been given, though the water of baptism had already been given to many.

This also explains another passage that you likewise fail to understand, where it is written: "Drink water from your own vessels and from the springs of your own wells, and let the spring of your water be your own, and let no stranger share it with you. Let your waters not overflow outside, but let your waters run through your broad streets." This passage does not commend visible baptism, which even strangers can have, that is, those who will not possess the kingdom of God. Rather, it commends the gift of the Holy Spirit, which belongs only to those who will reign with Christ for ever, since "the love of God," as the apostle says, "has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us." For the very breadth of heart that love produces is signified by the word "broad streets." That is why he says love is "poured out," and why he speaks thus to the Corinthians: "Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged."

So what we hear plainly in "Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirit that is from God," we hear figuratively in "Keep away from strange water, and do not drink from a strange spring." And what we hear plainly in "The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us," we hear figuratively in "Let the spring of your water be your own, and let no stranger share it with you." Strangers can have many gifts of God. They have not only those we share with stones and trees, such as existence and vitality, and not only those we share with cattle, such as breathing and sensation, but also greater gifts that belong to human beings alone, such as reason, speech, countless useful arts and much else. Strangers even have some of the gifts that were given to the house of God. These are people who will not possess the kingdom of God, to whom it will be said at the end, "I do not know you," even when they have said, "In your name we prophesied and did many mighty works." For, he says, "though I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and though I have all faith so that I could move mountains, but have not love, I am nothing." This, then, is the gift of the Holy Spirit that belongs to the saints alone, which no stranger shares. All the wicked and the children of hell lack it, even if they are baptized with Christ's baptism, as Simon had been baptized. Heretics lack it too. They receive it when they come to us corrected and sincerely embrace the bond of unity. If they did not receive it, then even though they had Christ's baptism they would not possess Christ's kingdom, because they would not have come to that private spring whose waters run through the broad streets of the saints and do not run off outside. From that spring the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. So stop citing those texts, which you either do not understand or understand to be for us and against you. Even if they were stated ambiguously and could be interpreted either for us or for you, they would do nothing for your cause. If we chose to use such texts, we could use countless ones that would do nothing for our cause either. Plainly such texts only prop up a bad cause, if only by causing delay.

"Look," they say, "water flowed from the Lord's body." And how does that help you, heretic? "A great deal," he says. "For it signifies that baptism exists only in the Lord's body, that is, in the church." You would do better to say "from the Lord's body, that is, from the church," even granting that baptism was signified by that water, which perhaps still needs more careful inquiry.
